subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance, who late Friday afternoon called a press conference which turned out to be his version of The Gong Show.
In announcing the formation of a National Commission on Inflation, the minister chose not to set any guidelines for the commission to follow respecting prices, wage increases or profit increases. Would he tell us what, in fact, are the guidelines the commission will be expected to follow? Or are we to assume that a price hike of, say, 50 per cent will not worry anyone on the commission?

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION
speechtext:
If the hon. member would read the commission's terms of reference, he would see that we want the commission to identify areas where there is danger there might be heavy pressure on inflation, thus endangering Canada's competitive advantage.
We do not expect the commission to look at all the settlements and price increases; we want them to identify the points at which there is pressure on the system. I have great confidence that the commission, under its chairman, Mr. Renouf, will be able to discuss such situations with the people involved and persuade them that in the best interests of the economy they ought not to proceed with increases which have been judged to be too great.

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION
speechtext:
The minister is no doubt aware that the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity came up with some interesting observations about the source of inflationary forces in Canada, including the fact that one-third of last year's inflation was due to the fall in the value of the dollar alone and that much of the rest was caused by the high interest structure due to government policy.
In the light of these observations, would the minister tell us why he chooses not to listen to that body but prefers to turn to a new body which will, presumably, be much quieter and less embarrassing to the government?

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION
speechtext: I do not want it to be quieter, Mr. Speaker. I have responded to the wishes of the House of Commons that it be given greater powers of inquiry. This was not easy to do because of the relationship of that body to the Economic Council. However, we have adopted the recommendations of a lot of people who are interested in the subject by giving this commission the power of inquiry. I hope this will be satisfactory to the public. Everyone will be obliged to give information to this commission.

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION
speechtext:
If the purpose of setting up the National Commission on Inflation is not to bury the issue of inflation at
Oral Questions
least for the election period, would the minister tell us why the government has named Harold Renouf as chairman, bearing in mind that he was brought to Ottawa to bury the AIB? Is it not a fact that you want him to bury any meaningful dialogue on inflation in this country?

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION
speechtext: The hon. member wants to make politics out of everything.

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION
speechtext:
We can all take a lesson in making politics from the Minister of Finance, because every time there is an election there is a new commission. We have had five of them since 1969, and in that period the rate of inflation has gone from 4.5 per cent to 9 per cent.
Will this new commission-this illegitimate son of the AIB-be reporting to the House, and hence to the public; or will it, as the minister suggests, be reporting only to cabinet where ministers may suppress its recommendations if they are not to their liking?

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have directed the commission to report to the public when it deems appropriate to do so. It is within its terms of reference. However, if after consultations and negotiations with the persons concerned, these people still refuse to work in the economic interest of this nation, I am convinced that the Renouf commission will release their names. At the same time, it will be able to make recommendations to the government and we shall study them but all its reports will be made public if it wishes.

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have discussed in this House many times the constraints we have to face with regard to food prices. There are many factors which come into play. There is the fact that we import a great portion of our food and that the price of that food is set at the international level.
I merely want to ensure that when there are price increases, the public is satisfied that there is no gouging by anybody. The commission will look into such matters and report on them. Of course, we must admit that there will always be some price increases in any market economy. We cannot impose controls on prices only and ignore other sectors of the economy. This is why we have decided not to reimpose controls and to expose all the facts to the public.
I hope that the hon. member will support such a move, because both parties on the other side were opposed to controls. We are not planning to impose controls. We want the market economy to operate normally, and this is why we are giving the public the instrument necessary to ensure that it will operate normally.

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION

subtopic: REASON NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION NOT EMPOWERED TO ROLL BACK PRICES
REASON NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION NOT EMPOWERED TO ROLL BACK PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I direct my question to the Minister of Finance with regard to setting up the National Commission on Inflation.
Since this is the fifth body which has been set up in less than ten years to cope with the problem of inflation, and since the NCI is to have terms of reference which are almost identical with those given to the first commission, the incomes policy commission headed by Mr. John Young, and since that commission was a total failure in so far as holding down the cost of living was concerned, will the minister tell the House why, in the name of fairness and equity, he has not given this proposed commission the power to roll back prices where they find that there are unconscionable profits or deliberate gouging of the Canadian consumer? How can the minister expect a commission to operate sucessfully when he has already tied its hands behind its back?

subtopic: REASON NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION NOT EMPOWERED TO ROLL BACK PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government imposed controls in the fall of 1975. When I became Minister of Finance in the fall of 1977, we decided to get out of controls. I am not proposing that we get back into them.
The other problem is that you cannot give an institution such as this the power of rollback under the Canadian Constitution unless it is considered an emergency situation, and the government at this time has concluded that we are not in such a position.
Since we got out of controls in April, 1978, I recognize that generally speaking in the Canadian economy, both labour and management have shown a great deal of responsibility, and I think that we can hope for the best in the future if all facts are put before the public. We have set up this commission for one

reason, and that is because CSIP did not have the power of inquiry. They were not given the power of inquiry because the first ministers a year ago said that they did not want CSIP to have the power of inquiry. The government has concluded that the power of inquiry was needed by CSIP, but as we could not give this power to CSIP we created a new institution.

subtopic: REASON NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION NOT EMPOWERED TO ROLL BACK PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. Mr. Renouf, chairman of the NCI, is quoted in the press as saying that this organization does not propose to require companies or unions to report quarterly on prices and profits, nor does it intend to have access to the confidential information in the possession of Statistics Canada.
Not talking about controls, but talking about gouging the Canadian housewife because of the fact that previous royal commissions have shown that the difference between the price the farmer receives and the price the customer pays in the store cannot be justified, I should like to ask the minister how he proposes that this commission or the government will find out who is gouging the public-whether it is the processor, the distributor, the wholesaler or the retailer-unless they get the information which Mr. Renouf says they are not going to require?
Is this body he is setting up not only to be toothless but also unable to see out of one eye and to be prevented from seeing out of the other one?

subtopic: REASON NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION NOT EMPOWERED TO ROLL BACK PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Renouf, as head of the AIB, had two inquiries in the last twelve months about profits of the food chains and has seen that the profit margin is nothing abnormal according to the present situation. He will keep monitoring that situation.
Mr. Renouf said that he does not expect to use his power of inquiry very often because he found when he was managing the AIB that the great majority of institutions were quite willing to give him the information he needed. He has the power, however, and I am sure he will use it in cases such as, for example, the president of Dow Chemical and others who have said they will not report to anybody. Everybody will be obliged to report to him, and those who do not will be forced to do so under the law.

subtopic: REASON NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION NOT EMPOWERED TO ROLL BACK PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a final supplementary question. What does this board have the power to do about specific cases of gouging? I would point out to the minister two instances of this. The first is the steel industry, where the workers settled for an increase of between 6 per cent and 7 per cent while steel industry profits last year went up from $196 million to $296 million, an increase of 45.6 per cent. The other instance is the banking fraternity, where high interest rates have resulted in profits going up by 34 per cent, or nearly $1 billion, and already in 1979 profits have gone up by 36 per cent.
What power does the board have in that situation? If the minister does not think it has the power to do anything, what
March 5, 1979

does he propose to do about calling in the steel industry and the banking fraternity and telling them they are the people who are pushing up the cost of living, and that they must do something about it? What is the government's policy, or is this board simply something to get them through the election because they intend to continue in their slothful state of apathy?

subtopic: REASON NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION NOT EMPOWERED TO ROLL BACK PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we stated in the fall of 1977 that we would return to a market economy, and I do indeed recall that at that time the NDP and the Progressive Conservative party wanted a return to a market economy. That is what we have at present. As for certain aspects of profits, it is normal that companies make profits in a market system, as capital is entitled to dividends, the same way as workers. The question is to ensure that there are no abuses and that is what the commission will do. As for bankers, hon. members will recall, Mr. Speaker, that a few weeks ago, for example, a bank announced that it would raise interest rates for Chargex cards. Following our representations, it reduced these rates. As for bank profits, there was a problem in our system, that we called income debentures, and in our November 16 budget, we eliminated this system by which banks could make profits we found excessive, and the House will be asked to ratify this through the estimates that are presently before the House.

subsubtopic: ALASKA HIGHWAY PIPELINE-POSSIBLE DATE OF CONSTRUCTION-DISCUSSIONS WITH PRESIDENT CARTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the right hon. Prime Minister.
During his very recent trip to Washington, the Prime Minister seems to have obtained from President Carter the assurance that the American government will soon undertake the construction of the Alaska gas pipeline. Can the right hon. Prime Minister tell us whether, in addition to that promise, President Carter gave an idea of the date around which construction would start, and whether the American President asked something in exchange, such as shipments or exports of natural gas from Canada to the United States?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ALASKA HIGHWAY PIPELINE-POSSIBLE DATE OF CONSTRUCTION-DISCUSSIONS WITH PRESIDENT CARTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it must be understood that President Carter and myself share the same point of view on the whole energy problem. Recent events in Iran have shown us all, I believe, that the problem of the security of supply, the problem of prices can constitute a serious threat unless we take defensive steps and creative measures for the future. It is in that context that President Carter assured me that the American administration would do everything in its power for that pipeline to go ahead, and reassured us that there were no ulterior motives on its part
Oral Questions
because the urgency of the problem had been demonstrated over there just as it was here through the desire of both governments, his and ours, to put in place legislation that would allow us to have a rationing system eventually. We hope we will not have to do so, but the legislation is necessary. It is now before a committee of the House and we trust we will have the co-operation of all parties to expedite passage of that bill.
As for the question of the hon. member on something in exchange, the answer is no. We, of course, discussed eventual exports, but no new project or new contract has been signed or is being planned between the United States and Canada. I took exactly the stand that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources upheld here in the House after the report of the National Energy Board was published.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Labour, I would like to direct a question to the Postmaster General. The mediator-arbitrator appointed by the House under the back-to-work legislation which terminated the postal strike was given 90 days to file the first report with the Minister of Labour. Mr. Speaker, I think the answer is rather simple. The mediator-arbitrator was nominated by Bill C-8 through the Ministry of Labour. According to the law, he has the right to ask for extensions to his mandate if he needs time to study the facts and to meet the people necessary in order to complete his arbitration award.
I think the question should be asked of Judge Tremblay as to why an extension was asked for. Apparently the mediator-arbitrator needs time to clarify a few items and to meet some people from both sides, namely, representatives of the employers and employees. I hope he will get his report out as soon as possible. I have no other answer than that, sir.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE ON PARTICIPATION OF WOMEN IN WORK FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. The minister said in Toronto recently that the job shortage is partly a result of the increased participation of women in the work force over the past few years. In particular he said, "We expect this rapid increase will taper off in the future".
Since previous estimates by his department were so woefully wrong with regard to participation rates for women, necessitating a report to the first ministers' conference last November because of its previous wrong projections, a statement that the department had underestimated to some extent the future of females and hence the aggregate participation rate-causing, I might say, untold hardship for women through the cutback by his colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration- can the minister now indicate on what he bases this projected decrease in the rate of entry of women into the work force? Is this a direction that his department is now promoting or supporting?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE ON PARTICIPATION OF WOMEN IN WORK FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the rate of increase has been very high in the last few years. We do not object to it. We have said it is a fact we have to live with, that there are more women coming into the labour force than before. We welcome that. However, it is a problem for the total economy: we have to create an equivalent number of jobs to accommodate this increase.
The participation rate has increased very rapidly over the past four or five years. It is evident that at some time it will taper off. When you compare the spread in most of the developed nations, it is evident that ten years ago in Canada the participation rate of women in the labour force was lower than in the United States and in European countries. The gap between Canada and the United States is now virtually nil. It is evident from that the acceleration will stop very soon.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE ON PARTICIPATION OF WOMEN IN WORK FORCE
speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Minister of Finance. I want to ask about a couple of specific price increases and what the commission will do about them.
Price increases have been brought to my attention by housewives who have been shopping. In the last six months, the price of raisins in this country has more than doubled. That is based on information that the wholesale price has gone up by 74 cents a pound and the retail price in Toronto by $1.64 a pound. Therefore, the rip-off is a 90 cents a pound increase in six months. What, specifically, can the National Commission on Inflation do about such an obvious rip-off as is now occurring with regard to raisins in this country?

subtopic: NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION-POWER TO PREVENT EXCESSIVE PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has concluded that it is a rip-off. There are many factors that do not show in a price increase. Most of the time the biggest part of the price increase is because the goods are imported and the price abroad has increased faster than in Canada. We want to make sure retailers in Canada do not abuse their position.
The AIB made a review of this during the summer, and another review last month. They concluded that, generally speaking, the mark-up by retailers in relation to their sales has not increased in the last while. If the hon. member has proof of a rip-off, he should give that to the commission, which will certainly investigate. The hon. member makes the sweeping statement that it is always a rip-off. I think the rip-off is probably very much in his own mind.

subtopic: NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION-POWER TO PREVENT EXCESSIVE PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not talking about a general situation; I am talking about something specific. The wholesale price has gone up by 74 cents a pound and the retail price in Toronto has gone up by $1.64. The difference between the Canadian wholesale price and the retail price is 90 cents. That has occurred in the last six months. This is the Canadian dollar; it does not concern imports.
What will the new commission do about specific charges such as this? Why does the minister not give them the power, not for a general control on prices but to stop gouging of this sort where it finds that gouging has indeed occurred?

subtopic: NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION-POWER TO PREVENT EXCESSIVE PRICE INCREASES

The House resumed, from Friday, March 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet that Bill C-29, to amend the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and to make other related amendments, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, as is the case on every occasion when we discuss the topic of housing in the House, I take the opportunity to remind my friends and colleagues of some of the difficulties and problems experienced by a significant segment of our society in respect of the critical shortage of living space. It is left to me in this debate to articulate these problems, which affect about 20 per cent of our population, and particularly that part of our population which lives in rural areas and which is of native ancestry.
It appears to me that the more changes and amendments this government makes, the more things stay the same. Almost every day we are treated to fundamental changes in the orientation of government departments. The UIC and manpower problems have been reoriented from what they were in 1968 when the present government took over. Last week we had a reorganization bill before the House which reorganized the Department of the Environment, taking away from it the Department of Fisheries and establishing it as an autonomous agency. Today we heard the minister say that we have reorganized the food monitoring agency from what it was three or four years ago-twice during that time the government has developed a new awareness of this crucial problem-and now we are treated to yet another agency. In housing, the more improvements this government claims the worse things seem to get.

March 5, 1979
Housing
My colleagues have been treating the House to horror stories of government programs which have failed, of hardship and deprivation suffered by Canadians, not just those in the poorer income categories but also those in the middle income category, people who are stuck with AHOP housing and who thought at one time that they were entitled, as are most other Canadians, by virtue of owning their house, to having a cushion against inflation. These stories are on the record and they should be recommended reading not just to our colleagues in the House but to all Canadians.
I have listened carefully and attentively to the points the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) made in his opening remarks. He has not been present in the debate in the House since that time and he is not in the House today. I suppose he is out conducting another Gallup poll in respect of housing, because the statistics he laid before the House are mainly those that were given to him as a result of a Gallup poll.
The minister said that there is a new awareness in the government of the crucial problems facing us in respect of housing. He said, for instance, that the provisions in this bill address specifically our great national objectives, the first of which is probably the most important, namely, the considerable increase in the number of housing units which meet the needs of Canadians with lowest incomes. Further on in his speech he identified that need as being an immediate need for 30,000 housing units in one year. He said further:
Our present housing programs, which are undertaken in conjunction with the provincial governments, hardly provide at the moment 19,000 units a year; it is not enough to meet the needs of the country. It is obvious that we must build each year a greater number of units for old and low income people.
I am almost compelled to accuse the minister of misleading the House. It was nonsense for the minister to say that 19,000 new housing units for low income Canadians have been built. Further, the minister indicated that during the last four years housing starts in Canada reached an average of nearly 250,000 units, and that that is not sufficient. He described in glowing terms the government's record in its past performance. One almost began to wonder, as the minister was speaking both inside and outside the House, what the reason is for another change in housing policy and another reorientation when things apparently were going so well.
It will be left to me to talk about rural and native housing. The program initiated in 1974 has been a total failure; there are no other words to describe it. In his speech the minister said that there were certain obstacles to the program and that he is confident these obstacles have been removed. Again that is nonsense. The minister is attempting to shift an even greater burden to the provinces. He is including the municipalities of the country in the housing scheme. The minister is creating more obstacles than he is removing. His commitment to 30,000 new housing units for low income Canadians in one year is nothing but a dream which exists in the minister's mind. It will never be fulfilled.
It is my intention to lay before the House the statistics regarding the government's real performance in the last five years. The intention is to shift a partial burden of the financing of low income housing schemes to the provinces in addition to a 2 per cent interest rate. There have been consultations with the provinces, but there is no evidence of clear commitments from the provinces or the municipalities that they have greater faith in the government's new orientation program than the last one.
Perhaps it can reasonably be asked why the government should play a role in this important area. Surely we on this side of the House do not have to demonstrate the need for government intervention in this area. Hon. members on all sides of the House agree that government has a very real role to play. Perhaps government members have been more skilful in articulating this need, even though nothing is being done about it. The concept of subsidized housing for low income Canadians cannot be argued. Housing is a very significant component of a social contract. Adequate and comfortable housing and the right to privacy are very significant components in the social evolution of our citizens. Of course, my party differs in its approach to the type of people who should achieve their right to proper and adequate living, those people with steady incomes and those with lower ones.
We have spoken about the deductibility of the interest portion of the monthly mortgage payment for tax purposes and a portion of the property tax which individuals pay. The government claims such a scheme does not work. There are many other schemes, all of which have been successful in other parts of the world, particularly in countries the government uses for comparison purposes in areas other than housing.
For instance, there is a scheme whereby individuals are encouraged to invest through a mortgage exchange corporation. That is something which should have been passed in the House years ago. It has been sitting on the shelf somewhere and has never been proclaimed. The mortgage exchange corporation would allow individuals and investors to invest in the housing field with the concession of not having to pay income tax on certain earnings from such investments. The scheme works well in the United States. It has kept the United States interest rates 4 per cent to 5 per cent below our own. Whatever scheme is used or decided upon, it must be one which functions. It must not be one which sees the minister getting up in the House every two years and proclaiming in glowing terms that the government finally has seen the light and that there is a commitment to do something about it, without tangible evidence that such a commitment can be fulfilled.
There is no difficulty in determining how people in the very poor categories should be helped. Surely the element exists in this country, as it does in others, which says: "Why should I help him? He has lived on welfare all his life. He is drawing unemployment insurance and is a burden on society. Why must I now build him a house?" One must ask what fault it is of the small child or younger Canadians who live in substandard dwellings because their parents have not learned to manage well. What fault is it of theirs? If we do not help

March 5, 1979

them, and if we do not make a commitment to alleviate their problems, they will follow their parents' footsteps and the problem will be compounded many times over in the next decades.
After 11 years of its just society, the government claims a monopoly on social conscience. I should like to give hon. members of the House an assessment of the government's record in this important area. In order to identify the people of which I am speaking, I should like to give a few statistics as to the seriousness of the social deprivation 20 per cent of our fellow citizens face.
Approximately 20 per cent of the poor in our country, or the lowest 20 per cent of income earners, have seen their family incomes decline by 7 per cent since the just society was declared. I am not drawing these statistics out of the air; they come from the government's record. That 20 per cent at the lower end of the economic scale earns 4.4 per cent of the nation's income. Incidentally the upper 20 per cent, the highest 20 per cent of income earners, earns 42.2 per cent of the nation's income. Be it in industrial negotiations or be it in the government's commitments to its public servants and social contracts, its commitments always are based upon percentages. If a family lives on an income of $8,000 a year and if the increment is to be 5 per cent, the family can expect its income to increase by $400. If we talk about the persons who earn $40,000 annually, their increments, of course, would be five times higher, or $2,000 a year. Incidentally, there are many persons in Canada who earn $40,000, most of them being in the public service. Both these groups of people buy their bread, lettuce, meat and steaks from the same stores. Perhaps I should not refer to steaks because the first group of which I speak are not buying steaks. Both these groups are buying their essential commodities and services from the same stores but their incomes are 500 per cent apart.
The rich in the country have been getting richer; the poor have been getting poorer. The inner circle of the just society is getting smaller and smaller all the time. Also the living space of that important sector of society, that 20 per cent of low income Canadians, is getting smaller.
Let me demonstrate how serious this problem is. I draw attention to a press report in the Toronto Sun. I am sure hon. members will say immediately that it is a scandalous report, a scandalous paper. But let me put on record what it says in the Toronto Sun and set it against a press release I received in my office today from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner). I quote the Sun:
Edmonton, Alberta:
A doctor in the small town of High Level has suggested that bad housing conditions may be a contributing factor in the deaths of three Indian babies in the remote village of Assumption from an ailment similar to the so-called "Naples Dark Disease".
Dr. Doreen Mitchinson who makes weekly visits to the nursing station in Assumption, said housing conditions there are "far from ideal."
Housing
What an understatement that is!
The houses are mostly wooden and they can be very drafty with just a wood-burning stove to heat them.
"Sometimes there can be 10 to 13 people living in a one-room house with two or three babies under a year under the same roof. It predisposes the children to more illness."
There was not a great outcry when the electronic media exposed the story briefly one night but it drew my attention and I did some research in the press. The only mention I could find was in the Toronto Sun. It picked up this horror story comparing housing conditions in our country with the poorest slums in Italy. What an indictment! Some people were upset; some people were ashamed. The minister sent us a press release and I want to put a portion of it on record. He said:
There is no question that health problems such as respiratory disease are related to poor housing and overcrowding.
The communities where these deaths have occurred are all too symptomatic of reserve housing conditions in general, but particularly in remote areas.
Unfortunately, the Indian housing program, like virtually all other government programs, is under severe financial pressure. I do, however, intend to review the situation to see what further action may be possible within limited resources.
The only word I know to describe that situation is "incredible". The minister is quoting need for restraint at a time when we are confronted with a further 8.9 per cent increase in projected spending for the coming year, at a time when we see no attempt being made to curb spending in the non-productive sectors of the economy, at a time when we see no curbing of the government's appetite to continue with its frivolous dream. It is left to me, as I say, to make the case for 20 per cent of Canadian citizens, the category which includes natives and non-status Indians. The government's record in this regard is one of negligence-one is tempted to say, of criminal negligence.
It is not that the government is unaware of the problem. In 1968, as I have mentioned, great pronouncements were made concerning commitments to establish equity and bring these Canadians into the mainstream of the national life. Task forces were set up and voluminous reports were issued. The Hellyer report is one example. The Rheaume commission also travelled across the country examining this problem. Mountains of submissions were received from native councils and people interested in social affairs, all saying that something needed to be done, that something needed to be done immediately, that something needed to be done desperately, to establish a greater degree of equity in this regard.
Then, of course, the government had its own reports. I have one here, a voluminous document containing some 62 pages and entitled "Revised Draft Program and Discussion Papers with regard to Housing Policy for Indians on Reserves". It is written in the usual bureaucratic jargon. I don't know how many times this document has been revised; it was probably drawn up in the 1930s and revised every time a minister felt the need for it or felt himself under pressure to make a statement. I invite hon. members to put themselves into the position of an Indian on an outlying reserve who is given this document, a document within which is locked the secret of
800S0-27

March 5, 1979
Housing
how he can achieve the kind of housing which 60 per cent of all Canadians take for granted and accept as a right, not just as a privilege. The whole of this document should really be put on record because it is a typical example of bureaucratic nonsense. Let me quote just a couple of paragraphs, however:
The Band Councils, through a housing management authority to be established for each band, would prepare project submissions outlining the housing program requirements, type of houses, costs, funding mechanisms and proposed maintenance procedures.
What a bunch of nonsense! Imagine the reaction to all this of members of a remote band isolated from the mainstream of Canadian life. Most of those living on the reserves are without radio and television; they have no access to newspapers, and not many of the older people can read newspapers anyway.
Another paragraph in this document has to do with training for the housing management authority which it is proposed to establish. The department would generously assume the responsibility for training representatives from the housing management authority in the "proper utilization of federal funding programs, the development of labour training programs and encouraging adequate design standards and proper maintenance procedures." A planning cycle is outlined. Can you imagine that, Mr. Speaker-a five-year planning cycle involving band councils submitting annual forecasts for three years as the basis for the preparation of three-year forecasts, two-year estimates and one-year budgets? Has this government ever shown any evidence of ability to forecast for even two months ahead with any accuracy? Yet these Indians are expected to forecast their needs for five years ahead. Here is another paragraph:
In terms of tenure, it is suggested that the Band Councils, through the housing management authority, hold title of the housing obtained through the non-profit housing program and that this authority be charged with managing the housing on an ongoing basis and seeing to the collection of rents/loan repayments.
When we deal with Indian housing, we deal with a very serious problem which cannot be addressed by contemporary bureaucrats. What we are dealing with is a cultural gap between the manner in which we in the House and in the country see ourselves helping our constituents and the manner in which the native community in our country hopes to achieve equity. This paper deals only with the problems of status Indians on the reserves. There are a number of most peculiar components to the problem which have confounded the social engineers and the public bureaucrats in trying to solve it.
Native culture is not taught in our schools or learning institutions where, for example, Mr. Teron or our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) received their education. The schools do not teach students about the cultures of the native people in our country. There is also the problem of the concept of communal living which says it is not important to own your own home. Even if it were important, so long as the Ministry of Indian Affairs and Northern Development retains ownership of the house once it is built, how can we ask the Indian person to make payments on this house and investments for the

future if it is not his in the first place? The house belongs to the ministry of Indian affairs or the governor in council.
In one sense this paper says that the band should have the right to own the house and property, but it also describes the needs of the individual with regard to ownership. What a contradiction! There is the whole problem of the high cost of servicing, utilities, insulation and building in the north and rural areas. We were told last year, and it is reiterated in this paper, that the subsidy of $10,000 which the department of Indian affairs offered to natives on reserves would be increased to $12,000 for status Indians who wished to build near urban areas, and to $18,000 for those who wished to build in remote areas. I am sure that anybody who has looked at the housing market over the last two or three years in this regard will not find it difficult to understand that this is just so much nonsense, and that with $18,000 one could not even cover the cost of putting the four walls up never mind the roof, furnace or water taps.
There are examples throughout the country of attempts to provide the most primitive shelter for people on Indian reserves as a result of trying to work within the constraints of these financial guidelines. The department of Indian affairs said last year with regard to the rural situation that, in addition to the $18,000, CMHC would be required to contribute another $28 million, Manpower to contribute another $48 million and other departments to contribute another $19 million over a five-year period to alleviate this crisis in the area of reserve housing. My friend and colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), will speak more specifically about reserve housing.
I would like to speak about the non-status situation and the rural situation which are as equally crucial and important. In 1971 the Prime Minister said that there is a clear commitment by the government to a scheme which would provide natives throughout the land, non-status Indians and, generally, people in rural areas with housing and that they should look at the right to own a home as an inalienable right in this country with the resources we have. I said earlier that the government has known of the problem. This is reflected in the Prime Minister's statement of 1971, but nothing has happened.
Another commitment was made-and I will not bother the House by going into the actual references in Hansard-in 1972.
Of course, it was in the early 1970s when the natives became organized and, out of sheer frustration, became militant. In an attempt to make their positions felt here in Ottawa they began to exercise some political muscle. Hon. members will recall that in September 1973 the message got across to the bureaucrats and the people in the policy planning group, and as a result a policy was actually developed. However, when it was shown to the Indians, hon. members will recall that one of the people who was charged with developing this policy and who had a clear mandate to negotiate with the native people was fired because he had discussed with them the intricacies of such a policy. This firing took place in spite of the fact that the minister had ordered the individual to
March 5, 1979

make sure that whatever policy was advanced to the cabinet had the approval and acceptance of the native community.
In those years a whole new science developed within the bureaucracy. The conventional manner of giving these people a snow job did not work as well because they began to take the ministers at their word, and every time they or the Prime Minister or one of the senior bureaucrats made a new commitment, the native people expected it to be fulfilled. Of course, when that did not happen the native people became very concerned, outspoken and militant.
Then there was the new approach-which really is not new at all but which certainly came in handy at the time-of dividing and conquering, dividing the status native community from the non-status native community, the urban native community from the rural native community, and so on. Eventually, however, a decision had to be made, and it came in March, 1974, precisely five years ago when the policy for rural native housing was announced.
This year is the fifth anniversary of this policy, and it is in this climate that I have the opportunity to speak on this matter again. Let me put on the record the manner in which the policy is described in the manual under the heading "Rural and Native Housing":
CMHCs rural and native housing policy, announced in March, 1974, attempts to marshall all of the resources of the NHA for the benefit of rural and native people and, specifically, within the next five years, to acquire or build 50,000 housing units for these people and to rehabilitate an equal number.
Over a five-year period there would be 100,000 new housing units. The manual goes on to say:
The policy is to encourage the people concerned to plan, build and manage their own projects as much as possible, so that they will acquire not only housing but new skills and economic security as well. The resources of many other federal programs are channelled to rural and native people through an interdepartmental committee, of which CMHC is chairman. At the provincial level, federal-provincial rural and native housing committees perform a similar function.
One innovative aspect of the policy is to allow rural and native people to buy their homes with monthly payments related to their incomes, on a scale similar to that used to calculate rents in public housing projects.
The natives had asked for 30,000 new homes but the minister, not to be outdone, said their needs were for 50,000. That can well be demonstrated by all the reports I have enumerated, such as the Hellyer report and the Rheaume report.
Let me deal briefly with the record of this policy to build 50,000 homes over a five-year period and to rehabilitate another 50,000. In 1975, after the first year, I asked the minister how many homes had been built. The minister had forgotten there was such a policy but he checked with his officials and two or three days later said 24 of the 50,000 homes had been built. They were all in my constituency. It was a project I demonstrated in my home town, because we have to start somewhere, Mr. Speaker. A year later I asked the question again. At that time, 300 houses had been built.
When I was preparing my remarks for today. I telephoned CMHC to see how the policy had performed. The information
Housing
service did not know of its existence. Apparently the minister's office was alerted and a directive sent to the people in charge of it to give me whatever information I wanted. I was told that 31,144 houses had been built over the five-year period. That was a source of comfort to me, as I had not checked how it was going over the last few months.
I asked where the houses had been built. My province of British Columbia was mentioned and the province of Ontario. I asked how many new houses in total had been built and was told that the 50,000 houses were a combination of new and rehabilitated houses. I reminded them that the program was to build 50,000 new houses and rehabilitate the same number. I read the minister's press relase to them, I read the minister's speech in the House to them and an excerpt from the government's housing policy. It was admitted that all this was very true and they offered to give me the figures on the new houses actually built. In the five-year period 7,753 houses had been built and 23,391 rehabilitated.
I shall give the figures for each province in order to demonstrate the kind of response received for his frivolous dream from the provinces. In Newfoundland, 1,824 houses were built; in Nova Scotia, 549; Prince Edward Island, 45; New Brunswick, 450; and Ontario, 834. The program works well in Ontario and Newfoundland because there are groups organized by natives to provide a delivery system. In Manitoba, 1,266 houses were built and in Saskatchewan, 1,549 were built. In Alberta, the province with the housing problem described in the story in the Toronto Sun, 405 houses were built; and in British Columbia, 838. There was no requirement for the government to make any deal in the two territories. Surely we cannot abrogate our responsibilities for the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Only 34 of the 50,000 houses were built in the Northwest Territories. In the Yukon it was zero; no new houses under this program for the Yukon.
I have omitted the province of Quebec, where the minister is the champion of federalism, the champion of all that is good and desirable in a just society.
Order, please. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Does the hon. member have unanimous consent?
No.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention will be relatively brief. I want to speak about two aspects of the bill, the one that relates to the more effective delivery of housing to Indian reserves, and the other that deals with the conservation of heritage buildings. They seem at first blush to be rather disparate elements, but one stems from my responsibility as Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the other from my mandate in the parks program for heritage preservation. There are aspects of the bill which will be helpful in dealing with both areas and I should like to draw the

March 5, 1979
Housing
attention of the House to those amendments which I think will help address the problem that has been under discussion.
If we look at the problems confronting the department in coming to grips with the very serious housing conditions on Indian reservations, I think we all share the view that a great deal has to be done. The hon. member who just preceded me, in a fashion which I think is rather characteristic of him, pointed out the problems, discussed some of the difficulties and dwelt on some of the shortcomings, but failed to mention some of the improvements we have made in respect of housing on the reserves in the last ten years. I do not think anyone who is anxious to be fair would deny there has been substantial progress. What has to be admitted is that there are still outstanding difficulties facing the department in trying to address the problem of Indian housing.
I think it is important to recognize that in the past ten years we have built approximately 10,800 houses on Indian reserves. In 1973-74, our rate of new house construction was approximately 2,000 per year, but as a result of a decision taken in cabinet in August, 1977, the rate was increased to about 2,400 new houses per year. At the same time, some existing 3,000 houses on Indian reserves are currently being renovated each year.
That is an improvement over what was being done. Although hon. members opposite tend to dissociate themselves from the past, they cannot avoid the reality that they were the government of this country between 1957 and 1963. They were not great years, Mr. Speaker, but the point is that they also had a chance to address the question of Indian housing. They also had a chance at that point to address the question of health services on reserves. I would ask any of them, particularly the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), to compare the rate of new housing in those years, the rate of new infrastructure in terms of water supply and health delivery services in those years, with what has been done in recent years. I agree with the hon. member that the task is still in front of us and, if anything, is becoming more difficult to cope with.
The housing needs analysis which was effective in December, 1977, indicated there is still a need over the next five years for approximately 22,500 new homes and the rehabilitation of some 30,000 existing homes on Indian reserves across Canada. There is no question that new construction and renovation is badly needed to reduce overcrowding, to replace substandard housing, and to provide for newly formed families. There is equally no question in my mind that the failure of governments, and-let us be realistic-the failure of this parliament, to find sufficient sums to meet this problem has contributed to the conditions which the hon. member I think rightly described. Maybe the tragedy he referred to of those Indian children will quicken the consciences of members in this House on all sides to recognize that there is more to be done in these areas affecting the Indian people.

I am dealing specifically with the status Indians. The hon. member went on to discuss the Metis and non-status Indians, and that is a question we can probably discuss in committee. The fact is there have been some achievements; there is no question about that. In recent years particularly there have been some solid achievements. The task is still there and it is an immense one. In my rough estimate, if we would try to catch up to that backlog, say over a period of five years, we are looking at an expenditure of something like $400 million. This is just to try to deal with the housing problem alone on the reserves. The present rate of expenditure is something like $195 million. There is a question of financing that is directly involved, but there is also a question of will and I think to the extent this chamber is engaged in a debate about this, there seems to be concern on both sides of the House that we address this question more forcibly. Hopefully when we get to committee we will be able to generate a little head of steam which in turn will lead to some money, increased appropriations, to deal with this very important problem.
Let me point out that Bill C-29 which is before us does help deal with the problem. I just want to go over the reason why. One of the main financing questions has been to supplement my department's $12,000 capital housing subsidy with programs from other federal departments. I want to tell the House today that after some discussions I think it is fair to say that we are in the final stages of developing a formula for using LEAP funds from CEIC, in a manner that coincides with the summer construction season. This has been a source of difficulty with the Indian people over the past two or three years. I think we are fairly close to an agreement that would allow these Canada Works funds to come in at the beginning of the season to maximize the construction period during the summer months.
Another important mechanism for financing Indian housing and for narrowing the gap between a decent house and what my department's housing subsidy can provide is through the provisions of the National Housing Act and its delivery agent, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. There have been and still are difficulties in applying the NHA to the particular circumstances of Indian reserves. However, improvements are being made, in particular some of the amendments proposed in Bill C-29.
The most important feature of the proposed amendments to the Indian people is the non-profit housing program, which is designed to increase the supply of low rent housing. This program enables non-profit groups and co-op groups, in this case Indian chiefs and councils, to develop the most appropriate form of housing at minimum cost to low and moderate income families and individuals. It is obviously potentially quite useful in the reserve situation since the majority of Indian people are in low and moderate income groups.
Many bands have been reluctant to use CMHC loans because of the requirement to incorporate. They felt that such incorporation would affect their Indian status and put reserve land in jeopardy. Amendments to section 15(1) remove the
March 5, 1979

major block to the utilization of CMHC programs in response to the particular concern of the Indian people which I have mentioned. As a result of amendments to section 15(1), Indians will be able to obtain all the benefits of non-profit housing without the necessity of having to legally incorporate as nonprofit organizations.
How the non-profit housing program works is that it provides a mechanism for obtaining capital funds for bands to build houses and rent them to occupants wishing to supplement my department's $12,000 housing subsidy. The capital funds in this case come from CMHC, but not, until passage of this bill, from approved lenders, which is the important addition. These lenders normally require some form of mortgage for their funds. Following the passage of Bill C-29 the approved lenders will be able to make loans to Indians for housing on reserves without having to take mortgages on reserve property. My guarantee, as Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, of repayment of the loan in case of default will be the security needed for such loans.
With respect to the non-profit housing program, there is already provision in the National Housing Act for interest reduction. Through an operating agreement with the chief and band council the interest rate on these loans can be as low as 1 per cent or 2 per cent. Thus, the payment schedule for the occupant to the band is only a modest amount. This bill should ease the problems that bands have in financing housing in this particular way.
Besides the non-profit housing improvements, the amendments also affect the application of RRAP, the residential rehabilitation assistance program. This program is designed to upgrade the existing housing stock in low income areas through a combination of low interest and forgivable loans.
Under a revised section 34.1 the amendments expand the scope of RRAP to cover all Indian reserves. Henceforth all Indian bands will qualify for assistance, irrespective of the location of the Indian reserves. Formerly, it was a requirement for participation in RRAP that Indian reserves be located in areas which provinces designated as high unemployment. As is frequently the case, Indian reserves with high rates of unemployment could be located in areas of otherwise high employment. With the passage of Bill C-29 this will no longer make such affected reserves ineligible for RRAP.
Indian leaders in Canada have been consistent in their representations as to how we must address the housing problem on reserves. They are saying that the authority and responsibility for delivering a housing program must be at the level of the Indian band council. Members here today will recall earlier remarks I have made in this House endorsing the concepts of Indian control and Indian self-determination. Our housing program direction is aimed very much along the line of this philosophy, although progress is often agonizingly slow.
The amendments concerning non-profit housing are designed to further the objective of placing housing responsibility at the band level. At the same time the department is setting up regional Indian housing councils to help monitor and supervise the implementation of the housing program.
Housing
Indian people also say to me that my department should be responsible for co-ordinating financing and programming sources for Indian bands or groups of bands. My participation in this debate and the provisions to tailor the NHA to reserve circumstances are a reflection of my commitment to respond to this co-ordinating responsibility.
Indian people are arguing that there should be a strong association between land tenure and the trust responsibility of the minister of Indian affairs. I believe in this context that Indian bands need to be able to develop mtchanisms for granting tenure without jeopardizing the status of reserve lands. As I stated earlier, this bill will provide greater flexibility in this respect.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we all have an obligation to continue to work with the Indian people to try to solve the problem of Indian housing, and to work with the Indian people in a meaningful way, because in the final analysis they may be and probably are the best judges of how housing problems on the reserves should be handled. I happen to believe that the bill before us in that respect is a contribution to the objectives I and the Indian people have, and of course I welcome them.
I would like for a moment, if I may, to look at the bill in terms of my mandate as the minister responsible for Parks Canada, particularly the national program of historic conservation and commemoration. You may not know this, Mr. Speaker, but there are some one million buildings in Canada which were constructed prior to 1920. These buildings are a highly valuable resource in terms of capital investment, the labour and culture they represent, yet many of these are in a poor state of repair and are often threatened with demolition.
The loss of historic properties and the destruction of neighbourhoods and streetscapes is a continuing drain on our national built heritage. CMHC is being most helpful in encouraging recycling, renovation and heritage preservation in Canada. There is an emerging policy thrust in heritage, and my colleague referred to existing practices in a speech to HUDAC last week.
This bill should complement these CMHC practices in the following ways. First, provision is made in the bill for obtaining funds for non-residential heritage property conversions. This means that in addition to financing the renovation of existing rental properties, the financing will be extended to cover, for example, the conversion of old warehouses to apartments where heritage improvements are being undertaken.
Second, through the RRAP program the bill will help heritage renovators by increasing the attractiveness of heritage projects to private lenders. The bill provides for insurance of privately financed residential rehabilitation under RRAP. This provision replaces a direct loan program by CMHC. The advantage of it is that in future, when refinancing of mortgages is permitted by CMHC, heritage renovators will be able to refinance multiple mortgages to obtain a single mortgage at first mortgage rates.

March 5, 1979
Housing
Third, the bill facilitates non-profit housing co-operatives by relaxing the membership requirements from the stipulation of 80 per cent to 50 per cent of members or shareholders also being residents. In conjunction with the introduction of this bill, CMEIC has been encouraging non-profit co-operatives to enter into the field of heritage restoration through the RRAP program. Thus financing will be made somewhat easier for persons wishing to recycle older buildings. Bill C-29 helps to meet the widespread concerns Canadians have for preserving our built heritage.
Other initiatives have been taken recently. The week before last, for instance, I set up a study group of senior officials from the Departments of Finance, Public Works, Secretary of State, CMHC, my own department and Heritage Canada to consider proposals and present within a month recommendations for government action to help save our built heritage. They will be focusing on tax policy, and in particular on possible ways to neutralize the tax incentives to demolish buildings. Tax laws affecting demolition are strongly believed to have unfortunate consequences for heritage conservation. This theme became very clear in the meeting the cabinet recently held in Toronto where we received a submission from Heritage Canada. That was the brunt of their presentation to cabinet.
This government feels that it is important to encourage the recycling of the built structures in this country. It is a matter of avoiding the irreparable mistake of wasting this important resource. It is clearly a waste of material, workmanship and energy to destroy buildings. The buildings we live in and work in are a vital and tangible part of our heritage.
Heritage preservation makes economic sense as well. It usually means renovation, and renovation is particularly labour intensive. Studies have tended to show more jobs created through investment in renovation than an equivalent amount in new construction.
At the beginning of this month I met with groups of professionals and businessmen and with representatives from municipal and provincial governments to discuss actions that the government and the private sector can take. There was strong support for the initiatives the government is now discussing. As a result, there is a concerted effort between the government and concerned elements of the private sector to consider ways to stimulate and provide incentives for investment in heritage structures. This group also stressed the importance of the role of CMHC. The bill under consideration at the present time is another measure to increase the participation of the private sector. The private sector is concerned about the adaptive re-use of buildings and is ready to act. This government is responding. This bill is an important part of that response and a demonstration that the government is determined to take action.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to contribute to the debate on Bill C-29, I cannot recall how many times in the six and a half years that I have been here that we have been asked to contribute to a debate on the housing policies of this government.

I recall the first time I spoke in a debate such as this in 1973. My advice to the government then to solve the housing problem in Canada was for the government to get out of the housing field. The minister of the day, Ron Basford, now a private citizen living in Vancouver, followed my advice to the extend that he got out. First he got out of the housing and urban affairs ministry. A few years later he got out of the justice ministry, and not too many weeks ago Mr. Basford got out of this parliament.
There are quite a few members opposite who should follow my advice and, along with the government, get out of the housing field. In fact, they should get out altogether. Maybe at the time of the next election the electors will take care of getting a few members opposite out of this parliament. They can follow the example of their former colleague, Mr. Basford, and take up private life wherever they happen to come from.
It is now the intention of this government to do something drastic with the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. Maybe the whole thing will be wound up. That would be good for the Government of Canada. It would also be good for the people of Canada.
Another time I contributed to a debate on the housing policy of this government was in 1975. I want to quote briefly from Hansard for January 27, 1975, page 2631, a speech I made at that time:
I have mentioned the basic problem in speeches before today, namely, government interference in the housing industry. I have cited examples of high-cost government housing, the need for money in lieu of shelter so that the individual or family can be free to choose their home. I quote from an editorial which appeared last September in the Vancouver Province-.
"-our housing difficulties, particularly in the rental field, compose a classic case of problem creation by government.
It continued:
We did not begin to experience real rental shortages in this country until the federal government removed the tax incentives that channelled a lot of private money into rental accommodation."
They have not learned. They have not done anything to reintroduce this incentive on a permanent basis. As a result, there is continuing confusion in the housing field in Canada today. I want to read another short excerpt from that speech:
Let me say just a word or two about what the minister himself said. He is credited with saying that the intent of his bill is aimed at increasing the supply and holding down the cost of housing in the low and medium price range both for home ownership and for rental. He says that if we are really going to meet the demand, we must draw much more heavily on private capital. Of course, the minister cannot draw on that private capital by himself but needs the co-operation of his government. The government, in the past two successive budgets, has indicated it is not able or willing to control the economic situation in Canada so that private capital will be attracted to those areas to which certain government ministers wish it attracted.
No action has been taken by the government to try to correct the situation which existed four years ago. Billions of dollars have been diverted to the United States. Expertise in the housing industry has gone to the United States. We see the sorry spectacle of Canadian expertise and Canadian capital providing housing for Americans. The government does not ask itself why that happens. It keeps coming up with more and
March 5, 1979

more programs, which reminds me of the old saying that we certainly have too much government in Canada, but thank goodness we do not have as much as we are paying for. We need only look at the publications of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs to realize where we are.
I have with me two booklets, one put out by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and one by the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. The publication put out by CMHC is a list of its publications, and it runs to 11 pages. The companion booklet put out by the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs contains a list of its publications, and that booklet runs to over 25 pages. It is clear that we have too much government, but the government opposite just continues with its policies and seems to think everyone likes them.
I think we should look for a moment at where we are now, six years after I first made a speech about housing in this House. We have the very same problems we had six years ago. It is true that some programs have been introduced. The government has given us an alphabet soup of programs. We have CHIP, we had DIP, and we have NIP. We have AHOP, ARP and RRAP, not to mention GPM, the graduated payment mortgage, about which I will say a word a little later.
In the last six years we have seen a dramatic increase in the level of interest rates for mortgages. However, people who are in the market for mortgages can be somewhat thankful now that there is so much money in Canada looking for something in which to invest.
Mortgages are actually available now at rates lower than bank loan rates. Mortgages are available at under 12 per cent in some instances, whereas the prime rate for bank loans is now 12 per cent. Higher interest rates, of course, magnified what was already the largest single component in the cost of a house over the years, but higher interest rates are understandable, expected and, in fact, necessary in order to attract capital for any kind of investment. If we reflect on the rates of true return some decades ago, we can see that capital was invested for a return of somewhere in the neighbourhood of 3 per cent. In the past decade or so inflation rates have ranged from between 7 per cent and, I suppose, 11 per cent. One naturally has to have an adjustment in the rate of return on capital; otherwise there will not be any capital available at all.
The high interest rates we have now are a direct result of the policies of the government opposite. The government has a lack of ability or willingness-I do not care which-to control inflation, the great robber. Why does the government love inflation so? The government loves inflation so much it is married to it. I do now know if we can tell exactly why, but one reason might be that inflation gives the government an opportunity to steal from the taxpayers of Canada. Inflation allows the government to reduce the value of the debt it must pay in the future, and this, of course, is at the expense of those who can least afford it, those on fixed incomes.
We might wonder whether it is really true that the government relies on inflation or loves inflation, but let us examine two of its current housing programs and see how they require continuing inflation in order to succeed. One of these programs
Housing
is the assisted rental program, ARP. After the government destroyed the incentive aspect of investment in rental housing it found, as it was told it would, that the supply of rental housing dried up. The government's solution was the assisted rental program. The purpose of that program is simply to reduce the economic rent for a rental property to what is called market rent. The government makes up the difference to the landlord. However, that money is not just given to the landlord. Even this government would not want to do that, so the money is lent to the landlord, albeit interest-free for the first ten years. Then the landlord must start repaying. If we do not have continuing inflation, the mounting debt created by the advances to the landlord in the early stages of the assisted rental program loan will bankrupt the landlord. I do not think the government wants all those landlords to go bankrupt.
I do not think the government realized what it was doing, but that clearly is the effect of the assisted rental program. It needs to be re-examined by the government and particularly by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) so that he can see the danger of these policies for the Canadian economy and for investors in Canada.
Let us consider the graduated payment mortgage, wherein payments by the home owner or purchaser for the first few years are at a lower than normal level. After a stated period, which is to be flexible-it might be three years, five years or more-the amount of the payments jumps up all of a sudden, presumably because the purchaser is in a better position to pay a larger payment later on. The problem this creates is that before the point at which the mortgage payments increase, the excess interest which is not covered by the initial payments has eaten into the home owner's equity in the property. Unless we have continuing inflation, home owners would then be in a loss position on the investment. If we do not have continuing inflation, we will have the situation we already have at some AHOP projects in which home owners simply have no equity. They treat what they have paid as rent and walk away, leaving communities in some cases to become ghost towns.
The other flaw in the graduated payment mortgage idea is that while the home owner may be in a better position and have a higher income five years down the road, all his other costs will have gone up too, and unless he is able to keep ahead of inflation by getting promotions and the like, he will not be any better able to pay higher mortgage payments then than he is now.
Having given a couple of examples of the government's apparent reliance upon continuing inflation, I want to say something about the effects of the inflation which the government has allowed to continue. We know that during this calendar year the national debt will rise above the $100 billion level. We are used to talking about billions, and perhaps $100 billion is a figure which some people can grasp. After all, it amounts to only two years' total expenditures of the Government of Canada. Let us put this into perspective. Let us divide that by the number of people. Let us get a per capita amount for that debt. That amount is about $4,300 per Canadian. Mr. Speaker, you and I may be able to handle our share, but what
