about the family man who has four dependants? If we multiply his per capita share by five, will he be able to come up with his $22,000 share of that national debt? The answer, of course, is that he will not, unless it can be stretched over a large number of years.
In the meantime we are now faced with interest on the national debt of some $8 billion. Translated into the terms of the current budget, that is about 15 per cent of the total expenditures of the government of Canada this year; 15 per cent of $52 billion is about $8 billion which we owe in interest on the national debt. That does not say anything about raising a little extra capital to pay it off. Somebody has to pay that off. If the present government is not willing to, perhaps they will be looking toward another government which will at least get things turned around and going in the right direction. We cannot spend ourselves out of debt, any more than could New York City or any other city or province, or any more than can any other household or individual. After all, Mr. Speaker, the government is simply operating essential services in the name of you and me; at least that was the original idea. For them to go on this profligate spending spree is abominable.
What are the facts of the situation? Where are we now? We hear a lot about problems in the housing field, the housing shortage, and so on. There is no housing shortage in Canada today. In fact, on the new housing market there are some 70,000 unlived in and unsold houses. Vancancy rates in rental properties in many areas are soaring. It is true that you will not find them in the densely populated cities because that is the popular place to live, but I can take you to many areas in British Columbia, and probably in many other parts of Canada, where vacancy rates in rental properties are soaring. One has only to look at the Ottawa Citizen, which I did this weekend, to find eight pages of houses for sale in Ottawa. How can they say there is a housing shortage? We say there is not. What there is in Canada today is a shortage of money. People who want to buy houses do not have the money to buy them; or, translated in another way, we can say that the problem in Canada today is that there is an inadequate supply of affordable housing.
I have to refer to my 1975 speech again because, when I was reviewing some notes for today, I found a gem of information there.
Has anybody else found it?

I think my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will like this because I am calling on the Canadian Organization of Public Housing Tenants for support. It turns out that they realized the problems which this government has presented to them and wrote the following in their official newsletter "The Raised Roof', the first page of which is headlined "the problem is not really housing". In their lead editorial they said:

The group has tried to show members of government, housing corporations and authorities that the problem in housing is not really housing, but the entire economic question, of which housing is merely one part.
Of course, those people know better than anybody in the House, that the sure answer to the housing problem is adequate money. Anybody who has enough money can go and find himself a house anywhere he wants to live. So it is a shortage of affordable housing. It may be that in place of all the expensive government programs we have today we may end up having to look at some kind of assistance. As I said four years ago, I have often maintained that the needy should be given a housing allowance to do with as they wish. Not everyone wants to live the same way and not everyone wants to live where the government says they should, in so-called public housing. I will be speaking about the experience of our friends in the United States and the problem they have had with the bureaucracy, with the administering of these programs and with the acceptance of them.
I suppose we can expect that kind of talk from a government which has a Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) who says a home is a luxury and that his government wants to tax luxuries. They have shown their inability to gauge the needs of the industry through their tax policies. I am sorry the Minister of Finance has left the chamber because he might be interested in making a few changes on this score.
Here he is.

The Minister of Finance has returned. He may want to consider some day the detrimental effect of some of his government policies on housing. I understand the ministers opposite seldom consult with each other, and on most days they do not even talk with each other, we are told. There is a situation in Canada today where the government says they are trying to encourage home ownership and encourage young people with young families to buy homes, and yet young people working together for their future are now taxed at the highest rate possible. There is no tax shelter they have been given to allow them to save their money to purchase a home.
There are some.

The minister is going to say there is RHOSP. All I can say is that the RHOSP with its $1,000 a year to a maximum of $10,000 was an absolute joke. Furthermore, it was not an incentive to buy a house because the only way one could benefit from RHOSP was to save money, not to buy a home. What kind of way is that to stimulate the economy? The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) and I told the Minister of Finance at that time that the RHOSP was a crazy plan because what it would do was allow the hon. member for Hamilton West, for example-
Balance budget.

So balance budget is the name of this game now? The hon. member for Hamilton West would be allowed to collapse his registered home ownership savings plan and go out and buy furniture for his wife's house which she had
March 5, 1979

already owned for 20 years. What kind of a plan to encourage economic activity or to encourage housing is it? In the meantime, through inflation and higher costs of all sorts we now find that older Canadians are being taxed right out of their homes. They cannot afford to stay in their old homestead where they have lived for 30 years or more and where they want to stay.
1 have dealt with where we are now, with what the old problems were and what the problems are at present. Now perhaps we should take a look at the solution. I am happy to say that my leader has offered a solution. Some of the details of it are well known. Basically, it is an economic policy with housing overtones and with very definite social effects as well. It is recognized in North America generally, but in Canada as well, that home ownership is the dream of families. It is true that all families will not be able to have their dream; nevertheless, the government should not make it more difficult for Canadians to achieve their dream. So we on this side say that tax deductibility for mortgage interest and property taxes would aid Canadians who want to buy a home.
That is not what you were saying two years ago in your riding.

What we have now is a situation where young people are not encouraged to buy their homes, which means a drain on the housing market because there is not the activity necessary to contribute to the over-all economic well-being of the country.
Why is the government opposed to our proposal? The obvious reason is that the government did not think of it first or, if they thought of it first, they did not get around to acting on it, which may be more the truth. The Minister of Finance says it is a program for the rich. It is obvious that the rich do not care about a program such as this. The rich already own their own homes. If they are rich, either they are without mortgages or they have assets of sufficient size that they are able to arrange to have their mortgage interest deductible.
It is a long standing rule in our Canadian tax laws that any expense laid out to earn income is deductible. If a taxpayer borrows money for the purpose of earning income, such as buying bonds, stocks, a revenue-producing building or registered retirement savings plans, the interest paid by the taxpayer is deductible. But if he borrows money to buy a house, it is not deductible. It is so mixed up that even if a taxpayer sells his home, takes back a mortgage from the purchaser, then purchases another home and assumes a larger mortgage therefor, the poor taxpayer must include the interest income in his income for tax purposes, but he is not allowed to deduct the interest which he is paying because of receiving this interest.
Under Canadian tax laws it is very important to follow the line carefully and not be confused. One must take the correct step at the correct time. Otherwise, the minister's henchmen come along and say: "That is not what we meant; you must pay". I know it can be done. I am a chartered accountant. I
Housing
used to do some tax practice before I came here. Now I have so much to do here that I can hardly keep track of what is going on in the tax laws. But any Canadian taxpayer who has any amount of assets at all can deduct his home ownership interest under the present rules, with good tax advice.
The minister indicated that this is a program for the rich. If the rich can get around this and deduct their mortgage interest anyway, let us have a program for the poor. We should let the poor deduct their mortgage interest, too. Let us not restrict mortgage deductibility to the rich. In any event, the rich have their houses; they are not the ones we on this side worry about. The rich who own their houses are not about to remortgage them unless it is for business purposes. In any event, they can easily go to the bank with their clear title certificates and borrow money if the rates are more favourable. One can be sure they will. The plan which my leader has outlined carefully throughout the country has been extremely popular, and so it should be. Canadian taxpayers and residents realize there is something in it for everyone.
Increasing the deficit.

It will help young and old home owners and renters. It will help the young who are either just forming households or those who are now renting and want to become home owners. It will mean they will have the benefit of lower monthly payments than otherwise. The old home owners, the ones being forced out of their homes by the government's economic policies because the size of their pensions and savings are shrinking, will be given the right to deduct their property taxes. It will provide them with a savings and help them to stay in their houses. There is no reason for the old folks to be forced out of their houses by some uncaring government. It will help young renters because it will be easier for them to make the transition from rental to home ownership. The older people who are renters because of choice and want to live in situations other than single family homes will receive a benefit and encouragement to move to condominium type residences or to convert their properties if it can be done. Condominium type residences would provide them with the rights of home ownership and would allow them to deduct their property taxes and interest like everyone else.
The hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston) participated in this debate on March 1. I should like to refer to some of his comments because he and I were members of the task force from this House which went to Washington. There were five members of the task force. We went to Washington to receive information on the United States experience with this type of program. The hon. member for Westmount started his comments by saying the following:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention in this debate will be quite limited.
I agree with him. His intervention was limited in content, but it was not limited in time. As nearly as I can calculate, he ended his contribution approximately 30 seconds before Your Honour would have risen to interrupt him because his 40-minute time limit had expired.

The hon. member pointed out that this type of program should not be embodied into the tax system, that there should be different kinds of incentives to encourage people to pur' chase their own homes, something which could be put on one week and taken off another week. That is exactly the kind of tax policy which has destroyed the Canadian economy. No taxpayer has had the opportunity of a program being in place long enough to know whether he is coming or going when dealing with the government.
The hon. member referred to the severe consequences of withdrawing this program, if necessary for cyclical reasons. If the hon. member for Westmount were present in the chamber, I would ask him: "What about the old folks who are having their purchasing power withdrawn by the government's economic and inflationary policies?" Does the hon. member not think there is a severe consequence in withdrawing purchasing power year after year? Of course there is.
Also the hon. member for Westmount talked about using a tax credit instead of tax deductibility. We have come a long way since 1917 when we had our first income tax approximately 62 years ago, and people are finally accustomed to the idea of having something deductible from their incomes in arriving at taxable incomes. It is something which makes sense, and many things are deductible. Hon. members have only to look at their experience as politicians to realize how difficult it is for the average taxpayer to digest the tax credit concept. We have only to look at the difficulty in our constituencies of people understanding the effects of a tax credit when they give money to a political party. The hon. member for Westmount is a tax practitioner. For him to suggest something which would make the tax system more complicated rather than less complicated, I cannot understand.
Also the hon. member suggested that there should be tax cuts for all instead of tax deductibility for a few. Then we would have no way of telling whether the moneys left in the people's hands by way of tax cuts would be used to stimulate the economy which so badly needs stimulation.
As my leader has said on other occasions about his economic policies, we want Canadians to take their money out of their socks and put it into stocks. I am sure that putting money into housing would have the same multiplier effect as putting it into stocks. The point is: the money is active and doing something instead of being kept in a sock or in a low interest paying bank account to be lent out by someone else.
Also in his speech the hon. member referred to a few examples and compared our system to that of the United States. But unfortunately he omitted several credits from his examples and perhaps did not give the information he intended. It has been eight years since the last tax reform which the government assured would give equity and simplicity. I am sure there is not a single taxpayer who would say that we have achieved either simplicity or equity. The policy of my party would give some sense of equity to Canadian taxpayers and allow them to stimulate the Canadian economy by encouraging the housing industry with the purchase of homes.

Previously I mentioned the trip to Washington. I should like to make some comparisons between the system in effect in the United States and what we propose on this side. The system in the United States has been in effect for 66 years, ever since its tax law was introduced in 1913. All interest costs, including mortgage interest, have always been deductible, as are all state and municipal taxes. So they have an altogether different system. In the United States an individual is allowed to deduct $1,000 as a personal exemption. In Canada this year the amount is $2,400. In the United States they have to deal with 23 million tax returns which involve tax savings as a result of the government's taxation policy. Translated into percentages this means that 26 per cent of all U.S. tax returns filed bring some kind of benefit as a result of tax deductibility; the others are satisfied by the standard deduction which, in the case of a married couple, is $3,200 in addition to the personal exemption of $1,000.
We also found that fully 50 per cent of home owners in the United States have no mortgages of any kind on their houses. Of the remaining 50 per cent, 25 per cent have mortgages on their homes but the deduction does not give them any benefit over and above the standard deduction. Thus, only 25 per cent are taking advantage of the policy.
The plan has been criticized on the ground that it contains no benefit for tenants. I ask hon. members to think for a moment. If we can get some of these tenants out of the homes they are presently renting and encourage them to buy homes, we shall be increasing the supply of rental housing or reducing the demand upon it. To look at things in another way, the effect will be to reduce or hold steady the level of rent which has to be paid for these units. Thus we would have helped tenants who choose to stay on as well as those who wish to leave by making it easier to move out.
We have heard criticism on the ground that the people of the United States did not really want this program but that once it has been introduced it could not be removed because it was politically popular. Of course, it would be unpopular for the bureaucrats in the government to get rid of it because those who are benefiting from the program like it very much. Incidentally, we were astonished by the size of the bureaucracy required to run the very many housing programs which are in effect in the United States. It is enormous, and we cannot imagine anything like it in Canada. But the tax deductibility scheme in the U.S. is run through the Internal Revenue Service in accordance with a simple procedure which does not require any addition to the bureaucracy; not even 600 people, as in the case of the AIB, and not even 100, as in the case of the NCI.
So there is what is called a reduction in revenues to put money into the system where it belongs without requiring the creation of an extensive bureaucracy along the lines that almost all housing programs seem to require. One figure I have here shows that the government was spending $250 million on housing programs in a recent taxation year.

What happened in the United States was this. We found a situation reported to us in which poor people who needed housing assistance from the government were living in homes which were almost palaces in middle class neighbourhoods, whereas the middle class taxpayers who were paying for this subsidized housing could no longer afford to live in housing of a comparable quality. Is it any wonder, then, that the middle class is rising up and supporting a program which will allow them to live a little better, when they see people who are supported by their tax dollars living in a classier manner than they themselves can afford?
The policies we have put forward will be accepted by the Canadian people. The lack of action on the part of the government in planning the economy in such a way that ordinary people can still afford to buy houses and live in them afterwards is an example of poor performance that Canadians will not accept.

Mr. Speaker, the bill which is before us today is both useful and welcome. I am glad to note that the sources of funds available for housing in Canada will be broadened by this measure. I am happy, too, with the heritage preservation provisions to which the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) referred earlier in the debate. They will allow for CMHC guarantees to be used in a more effective way to permit greater private financial participation in the preservation of both neighbourhoods and individual buildings.
In my view, it is of great importance that buildings to which special merit and associations are attached should be preserved. They enhance the quality of life in our cities, improve the atmosphere of the neighbourhoods in which they exist, provide a link with our past and are increasingly popular focal points for the renovation of our city cores. So this bill, with the possibility it offers for increased private financial participation in the work of renovation, is indeed welcome.
I am also pleased about the provisions which will allow greater access to funding under the National Housing Act on the part of Indian people. In the last few years we have seen situations where many Indian people refused to utilize the method of establishing corporations to take advantage of the non-profit sections of the act. As a result, the housing programs which are available to them are much more restricted than might have been the case.
In my own area of Caughnawaga there were over 1,200 men unemployed last year, most of whom were experts in the high steel industry. They were not able to take advantage of this large reservoir of unemployed skilled men to build the housing which was needed and which many people on this reserve
Housing
could afford, simply because there was no means of tapping the funding available under the National Housing Act.
These changes are very useful, and I would urge the House to pass this bill soon so that this funding can be made available for native people on reserves across the country who are desperately in need of better housing and who up to now have been restricted in their ability to achieve this housing because of the limited funding available from the Indian affairs department itself.
One aspect of the situation regarding access to funds available through the National Housing Act for Indian reserves which I feel the government should consider at second reading as a possible amendment to this bill is with regard to opening up the provisions dealing with land banking or land assembly which existed under the National Housing Act previous to the announcement by the government that it was ending this program with the provinces. This section is still in the act, as I understand it. I feel strongly that this particular provision should be opened up to Indian reserves. The reason is that many Indian reserves, especially those close to cities are experiencing the phenomena of land and buildings being sold at fire sale prices because Indian land and buildings can only be sold to other Indians. For example, in an estate sale, or where one must sell land for one reason or another, there is a limited market for the sale of that land. Usually there are about half a dozen people or less on a given reserve who happen to be successful businessmen or who have amassed money in one way or another, and they end up acquiring huge amounts of land on a given reserve. These are Indian people who have done well.
It goes against the tradition of all the Indian groups across Canada to have what was originally considered communal land but for which usufructuary rights were recognized, now being concentrated in a very few hands, and often acquired at prices which are unfair to the people or the estates selling the land. A very slight amendment in this bill would allow the land banking provisions or the land assembly provisions of the act to take effect, and if this were the case it would be possible for a band council to acquire funding from National Housing Act sources such as CMHC and thereby acquire the land at reasonable prices. They could preserve that land for the use of either the community or for resale at a more equitable price to other Indian people. It is a very unhealthy situation which is developing in this regard, and I urge the minister of Indian affairs to give my suggestion serious consideration. I will be raising my proposal again when this bill is before committee following second reading.
One other item in this bill which I like is the reference to community services. Unfortunately, the provision is not operative until 1980, but it does offer the potential of flexibility which will allow communities to do many of the things which they themselves have found are working well with some of the existing programs, such as the neighbourhood improvement program. This is a program which the government has decided to terminate, and I regret that very much. This program has done some interesting things in several areas of Canada,

March 5, 1979
Housing
including my own constituency of Laprairie in the village of LaPrairie. I would urge the minister to be most sympathetic in considering whether or not to allow this sort of program to continue under the new community services title.
Over the years I have heard a number of interventions by the opposition with regard to housing. There seems to be one theme which they constantly repeat. Perhaps the official opposition does not take the extreme position of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) that the government should get out of housing altogether.
That's what the board people say.

Nevertheless, the position of the official opposition to a great extent has been, "let the private developers do it." What they are saying is that we should let the private developers make their profits, let them speculate and let them do what they did in Toronto and around Ottawa. House prices in Toronto are approximately $20,000 higher than they should be and probably $10,000 higher than they should be in Ottawa. These higher prices have resulted simply because governments-and this includes our own because we do have some responsibility in the Ottawa area-have allowed situations to develop where land was acquired almost entirely by a small group of developers. The end result of this monopolization of land ownership around cities such as Ottawa and Toronto is tremendously higher prices for housing than are necessary.
You want more state control.

Since 1953 we have had on our statute books laws which permitted land assembly. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), who was undoubtedly responsible for the land assembly effort in Saskatchewan, is well aware of the successful land assembly program in that province. There land prices have continued to be among the lower land prices in the country around cities, and this is largely due to that government taking advantage of the land assembly provisions when land was still inexpensive.
Had this very same thing been done around Toronto and Ottawa, these two cities would be facing an entirely different situation today. These people who urge the federal government to get out of housing and out of urban affairs, unfortunately, seem to be having some success because we seem to be taking their advice. But what does it mean to get out of urban affairs? It means higher prices for the average home owner over the long run. Home prices in Ottawa could have been controlled by a combination of land assembly, National Capital Commission policies, government hiring practices, government renting practices in its buildings-

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF INTRODUCING BEEF IMPORT LEGISLATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing beef import legislation to establish reasonable quotas on the importation of fresh, chilled and frozen beef and veal, including provisions to relate imports counter cyclically to the domestic beef supply cycle, and to thereby assure consumers of more stable supplies.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that this is the first debate on a motion or bill to come before the House on the subject of a Canadian beef import law. During the last session there was a private members' bill that did not reach the House and there are at least two more private members' bills on the order paper. Needless to say, this exercise is a labour of
March 5, 1979

love that I am privileged and proud to be involved in on behalf of Canada's beef cattle industry.
I am proposing new legislation involving the importation of beef, such legislation to include the following aspects: it should apply universally to beef imports from all sources; import quotas should be established annually based on historical averages that relate to the traditional beef cycle as experienced in Canada and the United States; imports should be inversely related to anticipated domestic beef supplies, the quota formula should reflect a provision for counter-cyclical quota adjustments, and live cattle should not be included. I see no reason to incorporate a price limitation since quantity quota limitations that reflect our domestic supplies should assure consumers of more stable supplies of beef. There should be no need to increase the import tariff on beef. This is in recognition of the trade we have with the United States.
These are the essential component parts of my proposal and I will return to them in more detail later.
Hon. members may ask why we need a Canadian beef import law, why we should not just continue with the annual quotas set by the Export and Import Permits Act as was done in 1977, 1978 and for the current year 1979. There are a number of important reasons for this. Canada is the only country involved in meat importing that does not have such legislation at the present time. The United States has had a meat import law since 1964 and its application-or, more properly, the threat of its application-has been very effective. In its operation, the United States asks for voluntary limitations on beef exports by exporting countries to levels suggested by United States quotas.
I should like to deal in particular with 1976. With respect to beef imports and in particular offshore imports-that is, from New Zealand and Australia-that one year provides reasons enough for a Canadian beef import law. During that year we imported 183 million pounds of beef from Australia and New Zealand, an increase of 63.9 per cent over 1975. This represented the equivalent of 523,000 head of live cows or half the total cows slaughtered in Canada that year. The cow comparison is made because those offshore beef imports competed directly with our cow beef. If we had been short of domestic beef supplies in 1976 as we are now, our Canadian cattle industry might have tolerated this, but 1976 was also the year of our all-time high record beef production. By comparison, our cattle numbers today are about 18 per cent lower.
That year, 1976, was also the year of the infamous "six cents under" rule established by our government. This decreed that all offshore beef entering Canada had to be discounted at not less than six cents per pound under the same types of meat entering the United States. These price discounts were usually 20 to 30 cents per pound below the U.S. level for the same imported beef and of course established a Canadian ceiling on cow prices at what were generally considered disaster levels. Today, two years later, I am firmly convinced that the negative impact of these two items on our domestic industry was the major reason for delaying the turnaround in cattle prices by a full year.
Beef Import Quotas
Thanks to their import law United States offshore imports were 7.8 per cent of domestic production in the key year 1976, and only slightly above their historical average. In Canada the corresponding figure was 12.6 per cent.
Canada and the United States share the same North American cattle and beef markets, so it is essential that both countries' proportional share of these offshore beef imports be approximately the same.
The Canadian cattle industry has just come to the end of the contractual phase of its ten-year cattle cycle. The earliest opportunity to begin the national herd rebuilding will be next fall when more cows will be retained and increased numbers of heifer calves held back for breeding purposes.
More than anything else our industry is looking for indications of confidence and stability. The last thing we need is another year like 1976. That confidence and stability could be brought about with the help of a Canadian beef import law that would establish an atmosphere of predictable confidence which could only come with proper legislation instead of ad hoc, year by year, behind the scenes manoeuvring.
I mentioned the beef cycle earlier and perhaps some further comments would be appropriate. We hear more and more these days about taming the beef cycle. This is a noble and commendable objective but we should not hold our breath in expectation. If cattle producers and consumers were to learn more about it and understand why certain phases occur, I think everyone would be much better off.
The traditional cycle lasts about ten years and the numbers peak at the midpoint-for example, in 1955, 1965, 1975-and it is anticipated that the next number peak will be 1985. The beef supply-not the numbers-peaks about two years later. The expansionary phase will begin late this year in the current new cycle, with additional hold backs of cows and replacement heifers-mostly heifer calves. This in turn will still further reduce cattle numbers available for slaughter.
The 1965 peak was barely noticeable because of a world demand for beef, especially from new consumers, and increased per capita consumption on a global basis. That state of euphoria for cattlemen ended abruptly with the world energy crisis. Food dollars that had been buying the most expensive food of all, beef, had to be diverted to energy use. The result was a global oversupply of cattle and beef and the most rapid sell-down of cattle numbers in our history. That all took place within two years. It will require at least four years to rebuild and the process cannot be speeded up because of the simple biology of the cow.
The Canadian cattle industry is in the early stages of recovery from the worst crisis in its history. For the previous four years, prior to early 1978, lost equity in the industry has been estimated at $400 million.
The numbers sell-down has been greatly exaggerated by the need to continue selling at today's very high prices, and for one reason only-to satisfy our creditors, mostly bankers, who financed those four years of losses.

March 5, 1979
Beef Import Quotas
Only three other countries produce cattle and beef which can be exported to Canada in any significant numbers. These countries are Australia, New Zealand, and the United States. Mexico is involved in a minor way since Mexico exports some cattle and beef but only to the United States. South American cattle countries are not a factor because of our animal and human health requirements which exclude them from exporting to the United States and Canada. The beef cycles of those three countries are synchronized with our own. The 1979 calf crop, not yet born, will not appear on our dinner table for at least another two years. From a per capita consumption point of view Canadians consumed 112 pounds of beef in 1976, the year of our all-time high supplies, but 108 pounds in 1977 and 102 pounds last year. The 1979 estimate is about 95 pounds. This is two pounds higher than the previous 10-year average ending last year. I maintain there is no shortage of beef, but there is a lower supply than there was in 1976.
The base period in the proposed beef import law should coincide with this beef cycle in some manner. I suggest we should have a ten-year base period, say from 1965 to 1975 if numbers are to be the key, or from 1967 to 1977 if supply is to be the criterion. If a shorter half cycle is necessary to start the policy, then use a five-year cycle which is balanced on either side of the high or low points. There is already a probable exception to this historical cycle in that the new cycle now starting will last at least two years longer because of the extra time required to rebuild our breeding herds.
There are valid reasons for not including live cattle in my beef import proposal. First, simply because the United States law does not cover live cattle, our legislation should not try to be more protective than the U.S. law. That is an important point. We cannot expect to get more than the American law when we are trading back and forth. The Canadian-U.S. trade in live cattle and beef is a two-way trade, whereas oceanic beef imports are a one-way trade item. Canada and the U.S.A. are essentially net importers of beef. Canada traditionally exports feeder cattle and cows, mostly from the west to the United States. The U.S. in turn exports fat cattle and/or beef to central Canada. In both cases this only occurs when appropriate market price conditions prevail. Canadians should not forget that the United States is essentially the only market available to us for both import and export purposes for live cattle and beef. In this regard I am referring to our commercial beef cattle industry and not to the purebred side of the industry.
The timing of my motion today is most appropriate in that Senate Bill S-13 on the same subject is now before their Standing Committee on Agriculture. I sincerely commend the Senate for their efforts in this bill. I would say it is a logical development of their in depth study of Canada's beef cattle industry concluding with their report of October, 1977. This report is entitled "Recognizing the Realities-a Beef Import Policy for Canada" and was the result of their committee listening to cattlemen talk about their industry across Canada. In my opinion, this Senate study and report has quietly put to

rest the 1976 MacKenzie commission of inquiry into the marketing of beef and veal.
In his opening remarks on Bill S-13, Senator Sparrow had this short quotation, with which I thoroughly agree. It reads:
The hearings indicated that the most critical and pressing problem concerned the importation of beef into Canada, or, more precisely, the lack of effective rules pertaining to the importation of beef into Canada.
The hearings mentioned above were those of the Senate Agriculture Committee on its travels across Canada. Senator Sparrow went on to say:
Uncontrolled imports, without a firm long-term goal, backed by legislation, has caused numerous negative results for the Canadian producer and consumer.
As I have already indicated, I cannot support the inclusion of live cattle in this Senate Bill, nor do I feel that their use of "signal price" is essential or necessary.
Since my proposals have many similar features to the American legislation, some brief comment on their beef law seems appropriate. Last year a serious effort was made to amend the United States Meat Import Act of 1964. The 1978 amendment was passed overwhelmingly by the 95th Congress. It passed the Senate by a voice vote and the congress by a vote of 289 to 66, but it was later vetoed by President Carter on November 11, 1978. The amendment's principal clause dealt with the protection of producers during the liquidation phase. That is the phase we have just come through. It proposed to do this by means of a counter-cyclical formula. Live cattle will continue to be excluded in the American bill. The loophole in the old act relating to what they referred to as "slightly processed beef' would be closed. The President's veto was based on proposals to limit the President's discretionary powers in the proposed amendment bill. President Carter's veto memorandum ended with this quote, and I think it is very significant:
I am prepared to work with the Congress next year-
"Next year" in this case means 1979.
-to pass a counter-cyclical meat import bill which will provide the stability and certainty the cattle industry requires, while preserving the President's existing discretionary authority, and setting an acceptable minimum access level for imports.
That says it all as to why the amended bill last year failed to get the President's support, but indicates he is prepared to support a new bill.
With respect to my own proposal, I suggest that that provision might be made for periods when our Canadian beef import law can be suspended from time to time when conditions exist. I would be prepared to see that incorporated into Canadian law.
In conclusion, the concept of a Canadian beef import law has received wide support from across the nation, from government departments, both federal and provincial, from almost all cattle producer organizations across Canada, with major and detailed research and specific suggestions that have been supplied for several years from the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, and I am reasonably certain I can expect some
March 5, 1979

form of support from members in other political parties, including, I am sure, certain cabinet ministers.
We should all be aware of the joint policy statement issued by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) last March 30, 1978. They proposed an import quota policy for the next three years, that is, from the March 30 date. That release concluded with this statement:
If, at any time, it is not giving satisfactory protection to the Canadian beef industry, we will introduce legislation to control imports.
The "it" referred to is the policy.
The Canadian cattle industry is about to begin the rebuilding of its entire breeding herd after surviving the most critical period of its 100-year history. It is vital that this industry has unshakeable confidence in the long term outlook for our cattle industry. This rebuilding will take years. Let us not forget what happened to the Canadian sheep and lamb industry when offshore imports took over. Canadians today eat only about 1.8 pounds per capita of lamb or mutton. We need a Canadian beef import law.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF INTRODUCING BEEF IMPORT LEGISLATION
speechtext: Very briefly, it is a fact of cow life. It has developed over hundreds of years. Every country is now in the same process that we are in, that is, involved in numbers that they can import or export. It is not that every country in the world that raises cattle has a problem like this created by the cycle, only Australia, New Zealand, the United States and Canada. speakeroldname: Mr. C. Douglas (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF INTRODUCING BEEF IMPORT LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) on putting forward this motion today. As he said, it is a very timely motion, one which the cattlemen, the producers and the consumers are vitally concerned with at this time in the beef cycle.
Beef Import Quotas
Many times in this House we have heard complaints about the price of beef being too high, rising too quickly and everybody is to blame. I am not sure that anyone is to blame for the prices. The price that the consumer in Canada pays for beef, veal and produce such as that has remained almost constant in the past 20 or 30 years compared to the buying power of the worker. In 1950, he spent about 2.5 per cent of his disposable income on beef. That is exactly what he spends today. It costs about 2.5 per cent of his wages for the beef that he buys to put on his table. The difference, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, is the amount the housewife is buying. In 1950, Canadians consumed approximately 50 pounds of beef products per capita. In 1979, it is estimated we will consume about 95 pounds per capita.
The increase in the amount of beef and beef products consumed has been rather remarkable over the past 20 years. It is also remarkable that the price of that beef still accounts for 2.5 per cent of the total income of the wage earner. There is no lack in the amount of beef. It is the demand for that beef that has risen substantially over the past 50 years.
I come from a large finished-beef producing area in western Ontario. I have the honour of representing one of the largest beef producing areas in eastern Canada. Stability of price, both for the finished product and input costs, has a resounding effect on the over-all economy of the area I represent.
It can be seen from my opening remarks that I am certainly in favour of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. In fact, I am the one the hon. member was referring to in his opening remarks. I have a bill respecting the importation of beef which I hope will be discussed during private members' hour, hopefully before we are out of here. I hope the hon. member will take part in that discussion as well.
Like the hon. member for Medicine Hat, my concern is not only with stable supplies but with stability of demand for the primary producer. This is borne out by the fact that I have a bill, which will give to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the power to impose import regulations when in his opinion the economic and national interest of Canada would require it.
It is all well and good to say that we have a form of import regulation. It is true, we do. As well, we must have some protection for the primary producer. We should have legislation in place that can be triggered if a situation such as that which took place in 1976 should occur or appear that it is going to occur.
As hon. members know, the primary producers of beef in Canada, from the cow-calf operator right through to the finished cattle operator, have in the past three or four years come through one of the most disastrous slumps in the history of the beef industry. Much of the reasoning and the effects of that has been outlined by the hon. member for Medicine Hat.
In the industry they have what are known as cyclical hills and valleys, due in part to the producer's reliance, and I think rightly so, on the supply and demand position. That position can be greatly influenced, as it was in 1976, by a large influx

March 5, 1979
Beef Import Quotas
of offshore or imported beef and veal into an already volatile domestic beef situation.
To the hon. member referred to the Senate bill. It was my pleasure today to talk with the secretary-manager of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. While he agrees in principle and in general with Senate Bill S-13, there are two aspects of that bill which give the Canadian Cattlemen's Association a very distinct feeling of uneasiness. One aspect is the bill's reference to live cattle. The other is the reference to the triggering mechanism in that bill which gives the cattle producers and their representatives a great deal of cause for concern. It is known as a trigger price or signal price which triggers the bringing into effect of the beef import law.
The cattlemen and their representatives feel that a trigger or signal price could be misconstrued by both the consumer and those in charge of it. It gives them great concern that the signal price could be set either too low or too high, and thereby give an improper effect to the legislation which the Senate has proposed. I hope that will be thoroughly discussed. I understand that representatives of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association will appear before the Senate committee on the fourteenth, if my memory serves me correctly. Both of those points will certainly be discussed at that time.
The importance of live cattle has been dealt with by the hon. member for Medicine Hat and really needs no further comment, except that I believe we have to take into account the fact that the cattle industry supplies the domestic Canadian market and, more important, the North American market, which the producer looks upon as having even greater importance in the future planning of the beef cycle than just the domestic market because of the flow of live cattle north and south, mostly from the western provinces into the American system, and their return as finished cattle here to us in the east. That is an historical situation which has grown up over many years of good trade patterns between ourselves and our neighbours to the south, which could be disastrously affected if the live cattle question in that Senate bill is not considered carefully.
We saw what happened back in 1973 or 1974 when an embargo against the movement of live cattle was brought in- I believe justly-by the Canadian government, and we saw the reaction of the United States government, which I thought was somewhat unfair. That reaction included tariffs and the prohibition on the movement not only of beef cattle but also of pork, chickens, turkeys, and almost everything else. The United States reaction was very quick and almost disastrous for the Canadian beef and meat industry.
The reason mentioned by the hon. member for Medicine Hat for not including in his motion or in the Senate bill-and I do not believe it would be included in mine-the live cattle trade, is of vital importance to the Canadian consumer and to the Canadian producer. My concern is that while the instrument in place at the present time-and I will talk about it in just a moment-gives protection to the producer and consumer

in the short term, I believe it must be backed up with legislation which will produce the same type of production over the long run of the beef cycle.
Just what is in place now? The government took steps to establish reasonable quotas on the importation of fresh chilled and frozen beef and veal. Beef import quotas were applied in late 1976 and were in effect through 1977 and 1978. They are in effect in the current year. Quotas are administered under the existing Export and Import Permits Act. Furthermore, as announced in March of last year by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the government has an ongoing policy of import controls on beef and veal which will be in effect for a three-year period, at the end of which it will be evaluated, and alternative measures will be taken if necessary. In this regard I agree with the hon. member for Medicine Hat. I would like to see that over a ten-year period because the beef industry works on a ten-year cycle. This would afford the protection which is required and allow for the basic input which I do not think a three-year period does.
The current policy arose out of producer concerns in recent years, very justifiable ones, about the possible effects of beef imports at a time when low prices were causing serious difficulties in the industry. What that points out to me is that it was a reaction and not an action. I believe that now is the time to take a very conscious and clear look at the situation of our primary producers of beef products and to take action so that we do not always have to be reacting to situations which arise. The legislation put forward by the hon. member is that type of action in a time of comparative quiet, shall we say, when returns to the producer are at a level which balances with input costs. We have to remember-and not often enough is this put forward-that the primary producer of beef, or any agricultural product, is also one of the country's largest consumers. He consumes energy in large amounts. He consumes all the things the consumer in the city looks upon as being highly priced.
Many primary producers buy beef, pork, chickens or eggs from the same supermarkets from which city consumers buy. To say that they are not concerned about high prices is a complete fallacy. They are perhaps more concerned about high prices in supermarkets than consumers who receive weekly wages from Ford or any other industry in the country. Producers have to face high prices, just as inevitably as city consumers.
With respect to that I would like to point out to hon. members an article which recently appeared in, I believe, one of the Ottawa newspapers. This article brought to my attention the fact that we in Canada are not as badly off as some people would like us to believe when it comes to buying beef, eggs, or poultry. The article is entitled "Eat Up, Ottawa! Our Food Prices Are Low". This was not a Canadian survey. It was not one which anyone could say the government had rigged so that it would come out the way the government wanted. This survey is taken every month by the agricultural attaches in U.S. embassies in 15 countries around the world. It is impor-
March 5, 1979

tant to know the results of this survey. 1 admit that we do pay a good deal for most of our manufactured goods, especially imports, but the U.S. government has produced statistics showing that Canada is a world leader in something other than shovelling snow.
The article to which I refer reads in part as follows:
When it comes to food, we're on top of the heap, despite domestic price hikes and the plummeting dollar's effect on the cost of fresh produce we import for six months of the year.
Figures released this week show that on Jan. 3, at the height of our import season, Ottawa stores charged 21 per cent less than their counterparts in Washington, D.C., for a shopping basket of 21 items.
That must say something about the producers in this country.
Agricultural attaches at U.S. embassies in 15 capital cities survey local grocery stores once a month to determine prices for such staples as meat, eggs, butter, milk, tomatoes, bread, rice and sugar.
The results of the January survey published in the U.S. Department of Agriculture bulletin, Foreign Agriculture, help put domestic price trends into perspective.
The bulletin also compares the number of hours an average industrial employee must work to earn enough money to buy a given amount of food, based on mid-1978 Figures.
The February issue shows that although Canada had one of the highest increases in its consumer food price index in the 12 months ending in November, 1978, our January prices were 21 per cent below U.S. levels and substantially below Japanese and German figures.
The article cites the example of sirloin and refers to a kilogram of sirloin steak. If my mathematics have not gone completely out the window, a kilogram is 2.204 pounds. 1 will never get used to that. The article goes on:
Sirloin steak was selling for $5.62 (U.S.) per kilogram in Ottawa, $6.37 in Washington, $9.74 in London, $14 in Bonn and an unbelievable $41.20 in Tokyo.
The difference between Canadian and U.S. wage levels was almost enough to wipe out the advantages of our lower prices, but not quite. A U.S. citizen-I am speaking of the 21 items used in the survey-would have to work 8 hours 31 minutes to pay for the same shopping basket that a Canadian can afford by working 8 hours and 28 minutes. So the difference is 3 minutes on a full shopping basket.
What is of vital importance to the consumer-I hear people talking about the industry of the Japanese and the Germans and about everyone there being so much better off than we are-is that in Ottawa, for instance, a Canadian would work an hour and 2 minutes for those sirloin steaks, and in Tokyo a Japanese would work 8 hours and 11 minutes to pay for that one kilogram of sirloin steak. The question is the same right across those lists. With regard to boneless roast chuck, in Ottawa a Canadian would work 37 minutes for a kilogram of that meat, in the United States they would work about 35 minutes, and in Tokyo they would work 4 hours and 14 minutes for it. What this points out is that despite the gloom and doom of some people in Canada when it comes to the food price index, the fact is that the Canadian primary producers are providing this country with the finest food at the cheapest prices anywhere in the world.
Beef Import Quotas
What this motion is all about is providing the primary producer with an assurance that some of the valleys and pitfalls will be taken out of the cyclical endeavour and provide him with the knowledge that over a ten year period, or over the life of his input into the industry, there will be something on which he can count, should the need arise, to protect him from unfair competition-and I think in 1976 it certainly was unfair-from offshore beef imports.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF INTRODUCING BEEF IMPORT LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to compliment the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) as one of the few members of the House who has real expertise-I say that with sincerity-and working knowledge in his area of interest in the House, that is, in the beef industry. When he speaks I pay a great deal of attention to what he says. He speaks from his heart, with a great deal of experience and knowledge in the area.
I want to say at the outset also that I support the general direction of his motion, but I have one difference with him which is a philosophical difference because I do not think what he is proposing will be adequate to solve many of the problems of the beef industry today. What I want to argue for is a national beef marketing board, something that is supported by a large number of people across the country. As the hon. member for Medicine Hat has already said on many occasions,
I know also that there is a large number of people across the country who do not want a national beef marketing board. So this is a philosophical difference between the two of us.
Before I go into that subject, however, I want to underline a point made by the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Douglas), and that is that in general in this country we as Canadians are not paying an excessively large part of our disposable income for food. We pay about 15 per cent or 16 per cent for food. The Americans pay roughly the same amount of their disposable income for food, the Europeans pay close to 30 per cent, the Japanese more than that, and the people in India pay around 60 per cent. When we talk about food prices, we must put things into perspective. What we must watch now are companies, retailers and the like, taking excessive advantage of the consumer with excessive mark-ups. That is what we must watch in terms of food pricing.
Let me get back to this motion. As I said, I do not think it is quite adequate or that it goes quite far enough, because I believe we need a national beef marketing agency for two groups of people in our country, for the producer, in terms of making sure he has a stable price for his commodity, and for the consumer to ensure a stable price in the retail market for the commodity which the consumer is purchasing.
Let me offer one or two arguments in favour of what I am proposing. All we have to do is to take a look at the price increases in food across the board in this country. We find that price increases in products in which we have national marketing boards-we now have three and will soon have four in operation, the egg marketing board, industrial milk, and turkeys-have been lower than in products which do not have national marketing agencies to manage supplies and tailor supply to demand. One of the problems we have in beef is that

March 5, 1979
Beef Import Quotas
we do not have such an agency, and because of that there are tremendous fluctuations in the price of beef which hurt both the farmer and the consumer.
I could go over some of the history of beef prices, which has already been done in the House. Beef prices started to drop below the floor level, so far as the producer was concerned, in 1974. They became worse in 1975, and even worse yet in 1976. They stayed at that level in 1977, and it was not until April, 1978, that the price of beef for the farmer started to go up. What happened was that when the farmer was selling his cattle and getting less than the cost of production, he started to sell the herds. This is a normal reaction. We all agree that that is what happened. When a farmer or a rancher does that, he cannot replenish his herd quickly, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat said. This takes a long time. A cow has a calf once a year, not like chickens which reproduce rapidly. When the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) goes to the supermarket to buy a chicken, he buys one that is only about 60 days old. You cannot do that with beef. You cannot turn the tap on and off at will or at whim.
The result was that when we had an oversupply, the price was low and people started to sell off their herds. Now we have an undersupply. One reason for the oversupply was that back in 1973 the Italians and the Irish-the Italians because of some problems they had with their economy because of the high price of oil and because of OPEC, and the Irish because they had cattle which they wanted to sell-persuaded the European Economic Market to import fewer cattle from abroad. They persuaded EEC to curtail imports, and those imports were primarily from Australia. As a result, the Australians had to get rid of their beef somewhere, so they sent it in abundance to Canada, and that helped to distort the Canadian market and hurt Canadian producers. It created many of the problems we have today with beef in our country.
How do we solve those problems? I think only a partial answer is found in what the hon. member for Medicine Hat has said in the House today. As I said, I have a philosophical difference with him. I do not think one can deal with the problem of EEC unless there is a national marketing board, because unless you have a national supply-management board or orderly marketing, GATT agreements tailor your supply or production. You are not allowed to do that, and you need some form of orderly marketing, such as we have in turkeys, eggs, industrial milk or broilers. In order to have that type of planning, we need a national marketing agency of one sort or another. I do not think the type of import laws the hon. member suggests are adequate. They are better than nothing and obviously a step in the right direction, but that is one reason why we should go further to create a national marketing agency.
Another reason is, as I said before, that it gives the producer a more stable price for his commodity, such as producers get for eggs, poultry and milk. It means also that when the consumer has the product in the supermarket, he is paying a more stable price, the mountains and valleys are taken out of

the pricing mechanism and what you have is a planned economy, which is good for all.
Another reason why I am suggesting a national beef marketing agency is that we are not self-sufficient in beef and we will not be until we have a government policy which provides a guaranteed income for the producers. It should allow them to produce more of our own goods and commodities.
I have before me a group of statistics which I think the House will find interesting, and hopefully very shocking. They reveal a lot about Canadians which should be of concern to the House. The statistics come from the Senate. They were provided as background material for the consideration of Bill S-13, the Senate bill to control the importation of beef into Canada. These statistics are slightly different from the ones referred to by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, but some of the points are similar. The statistics refer to the net domestic production on a per capita basis in Canada. In other words, they refer to the net production of beef in the country. Also the statistics refer to the actual consumption of beef.
When one looks at these statistics, one will find that we are becoming less and less self-sufficient in the production of beef, according to the Senate. For example, from 1967 to 1974 the average net domestic production of beef in the country on a per capita basis was 85.9 pounds, and our consumption during that same time was 94 pounds per capita. It means that approximately 91 per cent of the beef consumed was produced in the country. We were 91 per cent self-sufficient. If one looks at the figures over the next few years, one will find the self-sufficiency starts to go down. The Senate had not completed the estimate or the accumulation of statistics for 1978, but it was indicated that we would be producing approximately 86.6 pounds of beef per capita and consuming approximately 101 pounds of beef per capita. That would make us 84 per cent self-sufficient. In 1979 the estimate is that consumers would consume approximately 93 pounds of beef per capita and that approximately 76.3 pounds of that would be Canadian beef. That means in 1979 we will be only 82 per cent self-sufficient. These are background statistics which were provided by the Senate researchers. They accompanied Bill S-13, which was introduced by Senator Sparrow a short time ago in the other place.
I have put those statistics on the record to show that we are becoming less and less self-sufficient in beef production. There is no excuse for that at all. We have the capacity to be an exporter of beef. We have a lot of land. We have a very small population. Farmers are in need of better incomes. We are in need of more jobs in the country. There is an unemployment problem. If more people were farming and producing cattle, there would be more people involved in packing, slaughtering, and the transportation of cattle. A better situation would be created all around. Of course there are the other economic factors of self-sufficiency as well, such as a better impact on the balance of payments, more economic activity and the like.
March 5, 1979

That is another reason why I feel there should be a national beef marketing plan for the orderly marketing of beef.
I should like to leave a few minutes for other hon. members to participate, so 1 will make my remaining points quickly. The heifer and cow herd in the country is being diminished. That is really a sad situation. We will have more problems in the future, and it is another reason why we require orderly marketing and more planning when it comes to the beef industry. The farmer is receiving less and less of the food dollar. A few years ago he received 60 per cent of the food dollar. Today he receives only 37 per cent of the food dollar. Anything we can do to help the farmer is indeed a move in the right direction.
My main point is that I think we require a national beef marketing agency for orderly marketing in beef, such as exists in the production of eggs, turkeys, and many other products at the provincial level. A similar agency should be introduced at the national level for beef. It would solve many of the problems of the producers and consumers. Also it would help Canada become ultimately self-sufficient in the production of beef. That would help every Canadian and the entire Canadian economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the courtesy of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) in providing me with approximately five minutes to participate in the debate. I am sure a good number of other hon. members would have utilized their entire 25 or 30 minutes.
However, I should like to begin my comments by indicating that I welcome the opportunity of making a few brief comments in support of this notice of motion. I do so because I have a great deal of respect and admiration for the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave). In addition to this respect and admiration, I believe firmly the enactment of the Canadian beef import law proposed in this motion certainly is essential and paramount. I participate in this debate to renew my commitment and support, because the intent of this motion represents not only the views and the position of the hon. member for Medicine Hat, but moreover it represents the official position of my party. In fact it has been the official position of my party since September, 1976.
The beef industry is a Canadian industry and it is a large one. In 1973 it became a billion dollar industry. Because of the increased value of slaughter cattle and calves, this year the figure is expected to exceed the $2 billion mark. It should be noted and stressed that this doubling in sales values does not reflect the same pattern in relation to increased profits. Rather, it reflects the impact which inflation and rising costs have had on the beef industry. It reflects the disinterest and the failure of the government to provide the necessary leadership. It reflects the failure of the government to manage the Canadian economy with any degree of competence or success. It reflects the need for appropriate long-term goals, objectives, and programs which will interpret accurately the market signs. Also it reflects the need to provide equity and stability to Canadian beef producers.
Beef Import Quotas
A beef import law, accompanied by a deferred annual income annuity plan and some common sense provisions in the area of capital gains, which has been spoken about often by the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles), would provide much needed stability to the Canadian beef industry. It would ensure the preservation of family farm management and ownership. It would greatly reduce and hopefully eliminate the government's sporadic intervention into the market place. Also it would leave the government free to perform only those necessary and proper functions of inspection, grading and dealing with animal health. Financial support would be limited to emergency and disaster situations.
In the remaining minute, let me conclude by saying that the beef industry, like food prices, has been studied to death. This measure was recommended and justified by Canadian beef producers two years ago. As I have indicated, it has been the position of my party for over two years. I commend the hon. member for Medicine Hat for his interest and efforts respecting this motion. I challenge government members to utilize this opportunity to pass at least one major piece of legislation before they strike out. I say to the beef producers of the country, if the government chooses to procrastinate throughout the remaining weeks or days of its mandate, we in this party will enact this legislation shortly aftr the next election.
