AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

March 5, 1979
Housing

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet that Bill C-29, to amend the National Housing Act and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and to make other related amendments, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was pointing out to the House the calamitous effect which the Conservative party's negative attitude toward the role of the government in housing could produce if it becomes government policy, as it did for a number of years during a Conservative government in Ontario. In Ottawa houses cost up to $10,000 more, and in Toronto up to $20,000 more, simply because the government of Ontario took a hands-off policy with regard to land assembly and land banking. I was in the process, at five o'clock, of explaining that even the federal government, because of what I consider was an over-sensitivity to provincial responsibilities in municipal affairs and an under-sensitivity to the national consequences of failing to use the many instruments available to control land speculation in the Ottawa area, has in effect fueled inflation in land costs and thus in housing costs.
The National Capital Commission's and the Public Works Department's land holdings in the Ottawa area, government hiring policy, and government rental policy or the absence of an aggressive pushing of land assembly programs in the province of Ontario, are all policies or a combination thereof which unquestionably could have substantially reduced housing prices in the Ottawa area. These higher than necessary housing prices, added fuel to public service wage demands, and the federal government's acquiescence to these demands unquestionably contributed much to the inflationary wage spiral that has affected the ability of Canadians to compete on world markets.
We have often heard that housing prices are largely the result of the some 100 approvals that are necessary before a house is sold. I would ask hon. members to reflect on this. If land assembly takes place surely most, not all, but most approvals would be eliminated because there would be a much more precise planning process. Many planning steps which are now necessary to approval would be eliminated, or would not amount to the kind of brake on housing development that the critics allege.
In the Ottawa area the federal government tried to do something about land prices and at the same time create a model city that would be a Canadian crucible for better planned urban environments, where public transit and various urban features like totally planned energy conservation,

recreation and green spaces, and ail the factors that contribute to the quality of life, would be imaginatively co-ordinated to show what could be done when the public interest comes first. In spite of the federal government acquiring 5,000 acres through the NCC and the provincial government of Ontario another 4,000 acres, the Conservative government of the province of Ontario, assisted by the sniping of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), and more recently some sniping by the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott), sabotaged the model city.
The developers who owned the undeveloped land immediately to the east of Ottawa where the Ontario government is approving housing for upward of 50,000 people, were considered more important than lower house costs and opportunities to show what could be done through planning imagination. Southwest city would have been a model for all Canadians. What a scandal, Mr. Speaker; what a tragedy that this opportunity was lost to all Canadians because the Conservative government of Ontario put the developers first and people second!
The worst mistake this government could make would be to follow the advice of the official opposition on housing policy, but unfortunately that seems to be what it has been doing recently. I refer specifically to this government's ill-advised and shortsighted termination of the Department of Urban Affairs. I will deal with that question later, Mr. Speaker.
I want to turn now to the suggestion made by the official opposition regarding mortgage interest deductibility. That proposition is as demagogic a suggestion as has been made in this House for a number of years. It is demagogic, because while it is patently unfair to everyone who rents rather than owns a house, and while it would cost the federal treasury up to $4 billion in decreased revenue-
Prove that.
There are a lot of people who are better economists than the hon. member and myself, who have produced these figures.
You cannot back them up.
I do not think the hon. member can, either. We are in about the same category as far as economics go- which does not say much for the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens).
Back up your statement.

The problem is that this particular proposition is very popular. I admit that politically it is very popular because it appeals to the selfishness in all of us.
The United States has had this measure in effect for 66 years. The group of members from both sides of the House who went down there to examine it, while they have taken public positions diametrically opposed to each other, heard one single story. I suspect they realized that the scheme does not make any sense, but it is popular. We all admit that.
March 5, 1979
You had better.

If we are going to be responsible in government, surely we do not simply do what is popular.

As I said before, the proposal put forward by the Progressive Conservative party for allowing mortgage interest deductions would cost the treasury a considerable amount of money. If we are to pass such a measure, it seems to me certain social objectives should be tied in to such an initiative on our part. I can suggest, for instance, granting a tax credit to Canadians over 65 who live in their own homes. Obviously, it is better to encourage citizens of more than 65 years of age to live in their own homes than to build old folks' homes and send them to live there. That does not make any sense. It would be better, through some legislation or other, to encourage them to live in their own homes where they are happy; it would also be more advantageous for the state.
I am also convinced there are other deserving social goals that could be encouraged by the government instead of having the type of gifts promised by the official opposition. For instance, with respect to saving energy, all governments consider that objective valid these days, but unfortunately the steps taken in the last few years to encourage energy conservation are still inadequate. I have two or three suggestions to make, Mr. Speaker. By offering tax encouragements and using new systems of measurement in co-operation with the provincial authorities in the field of electricity, we could save considerable energy. I am thinking here of a meter system that would allow suppliers to set the price of the electricity used according to the various load periods.
Why are tax incentives not used to encourage the installation of these meters in private homes? I think they would cost $100 to $150. If the federal government and the provinces used their imagination and co-operated, they would encourage home owners to use electricity especially during off hours and thus save money. That would amount to tremendous savings. The money saved would easily be enough to pay for the construction of one or two major dams, one or two nuclear stations. If the government had some imagination, it would offer tax incentives in this area. I could say the same thing about the opposition which, instead of making rabble-rousing promises, to say the least, should propose things that make a bit of sense.
I have already mentioned that I am unhappy with one piece of advice which the government seems to have taken from the official opposition, and to me it is one of the more mindless recommendations that has ever been made by them. I am speaking of the termination of the Department of Urban Affairs. This is a genuine case-and I know this is an overworked saying-of throwing the baby out with the bath water.
Housing
The government wanted to save some money, but it could have abolished many of the urban affairs programs which were costing money. I would have been unhappy had it done that, but not only did it do that, the ministry has been thrown out as well.
As far as I am concerned the Department of Urban Affairs has provided a number of important initiatives. I will mention them in a minute. But let me outline the number of international organizations that believe the area of urban affairs is important enough in which to be involved: the Council of Europe; the European Parliament; the World Bank; and the United Nations. Even the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, through the Atlantic council, has been involved with a number of urban affairs programs. And the federal Government of Canada is saying now that we should have nothing to do with urban affairs.
What are you supporting them for?
That particular decision to terminate the Department of Urban Affairs did not come before parliament. Its termination has been done by order in council.
By fiat.

I support the bill we are talking about tonight. This bill was introduced at the same time the announcement was made that urban affairs was terminated. That is why I am dealing with the question of urban affairs which I feel has the potential to influence, more than any other ministry, the kind of future Canadians will enjoy.
Vote the ruffians out.

Let me give you some examples of what the Department of Urban Affairs has been able to do in many parts of Canada. It is responsible for the initiatives that have resulted, for example, in the port front renewal in Halifax; Montreal's harbour front renewal; Toronto's harbour front renewal; the bicycle path along the southshore in my own constituency which engenders a fair amount of interest. In Quebec City-

-the St. Louis Basin, the Guy Favreau complex was changed through the efforts of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. The plans would have resulted in the creation of a white elephant. Thanks to the influence of urban affairs, the Guy Favreau complex will now be a valid and acceptable project for Montrealers.

The Lachine Canal project is another project.
There are dozens of urban initiatives across Canada that have come about because the Department of Urban Affairs was there. Surely there should be a realization that there is a need for co-ordination between different government ministries and between different levels of government. This co-ordination should be directed toward assuring a better urban

March 5, 1979
Housing
future, a better quality of life where the federal government plays a role, no matter whether it is in owning land, owning buildings, building new buildings in our cities, or whether it owns railways or wants to change railway lines. We passed the Railway Relocation and Crossing Act a few years ago which allows us not only to redevelop railway shunting yards in the middle of cities, but it also allows us to redevelop rail lines into cities for purposes of rapid transit. These laws are in the books, and we are neutering them, temporarily, I hope.
In my opinion, all of these very positive elements which the Department of Urban Affairs offered to Canadians while it was in existence, and the even greater potential it offers to Canadians in the manner it offers co-ordination between ministries and between levels of government, are so important that we are making a very serious error in removing a tool from our work kit that can influence our urban and suburban lives for a generation or two to come.
There are a number of other things I would like to mention. These are a number of pullbacks which seem to be the result of suggestions made by the opposition.

What shocks me most is that since World War II we have had the means to do better, but fearing too often to hurt provincial sensitivities, we have not dared insist on proper planning. We have not used our powers as moneylenders through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, for instance. We could have used this to force the municipalities and provinces to adopt better planning methods. Any hon. member present could give examples. Representing a suburban riding, I can give many examples to show that the need to rectify years of inadequate planning has given rise to demands costing millions of dollars. Had we dared use the powers our financial position gave us, we could have had an influence. If I may give you some advice, Mr. Minister, please do not be afraid to exert this influence, to insist on proper planning. It will cost you less in the long term. In fact, this is the same recommendation I can make for Urban Affairs.
It will cost ten times and perhaps 50 times as much to abolish Urban Affairs as to maintain it and-have adequate planning and co-ordination among the various other departments and government levels. The past often provides no encouragement. This co-ordination will be made without any incentive and we need a department like urban affairs to provide this incentive.
We must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that 80 per cent of Canadians live in the urban centres of Canada and that 6 million Canadians live in suburbs built since the Second World War. As I have just said, the quality of life in downtown areas and the suburbs suffers from a lack of long-term planning and co-ordination among departments and this lack of long-term planning and co-ordination has caused mistakes and deficiencies in municipal services. And even worse, the enormous cost

of certain planning mistakes has a negative effect on the efficiency of the Canadian economy and the capacity of Canada to compete on world markets. I mentioned the example of the price of houses in Ottawa which could at least have been reduced from $5,000 to $10,000 a unit if sensible action had been taken several years ago. This mistake on the part of former governments and ourselves has had an effect on inflation in Canada because of its unfavourable effect on wage demands by public servants.
The influence of urban development on our national economy, national energy requirements and the quality of life in Canada means in my opinion that the federal government must play an active role and contribute to ensure that federal policies and agricultural operations are co-ordinated at the federal level and with the other government levels. Furthermore, in the context of long-term planning, this influence will ensure the effectiveness of financial data.
I am convinced of one thing, Mr. Speaker, and that is that the Canadian people will long regret the decision of this government to abolish urban affairs if we do not take the initiative right now and suggest to our colleagues that the Department of Public Works take on additional responsibilities and that it become the Department of Urban Affairs and Public Works. In my opinion, this would give this department the prestige, the capacity and the talent required to meet the needs of our suburbs and urban areas in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I hope that the government will consider this suggestion favourably.
I regret that I feel obliged to criticize so much the policies of the government, but when a government like ours, that is a liberal government with a small "1", accepts conservative recommendations with a small "c", I believe that we must reconsider our position.

I am disheartened by this acceptance of a recommendation from the official opposition. Urban Affairs was doing a great job for Canada. It has the potential of saving hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars. This shortsighted step of terminating this ministry will end up costing us untold millions unless the government decides, upon reflection, to give the full power that Urban Affairs had to Public Works and allow that ministry the power to influence the co-ordination between levels of government and between ministries which is so necessary to help in improving the quality of life in the future.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the speech of the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) has been intriguing. I wonder if he would accept one question with a view to clarifying something.
Due to the fact the hon. member's time has expired, unanimous consent would be required in order for the hon. member to accept a question. Is there consent?

Agreed.
March 5, 1979

I thank hon. members. My question is simply this. In view of his burning criticism of the government with respect to its actions touching on the urban affairs department, may we expect some overt sign of this opposition in the form of his voting against the government or even breaking with the government?

Seriously, Mr. Speaker, if there were a vote on the termination of Urban Affairs, I would not hesitate to vote against the government. I support this bill because there are a lot of good things in it. This bill has nothing to do with the termination of Urban Affairs which will, unfortunately, be terminated by an order in council without consultation with anyone.
My further question is this. If we can arrange for a confidence vote on the question the hon. member is referring to, will he agree to vote against the government?

Mr. Speaker, I find that question amazing. My criticism of the government is that it has accepted the recommendation of this hon. member, the former mayor of Toronto and others on his side, who apparently have had it as a policy of the Conservative opposition for at least a year, if not more, to abolish Urban Affairs. My criticism is that we followed their advice.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to deal briefly with Bill C-29 which is before us. As I was listening to the previous speaker, I could not help thinking what nonsense we are subjected to in this House of Commons when he suggested that the minister should restore the Department of Urban Affairs to life.
I had thought that everybody knew that if the minister had eliminated his Department of Urban Affairs, it is because it was interfering too much with provincial issues. But that is the way Anglophones think. Another member of the House claimed that we should need this department to indicate to the municipalities how they should administer their own affairs. I am flabbergasted and I am afraid that with a parliament with such opinions, we are not about to understand one another.
Mr. Speaker, in all the projects the government has put forward over the years in the area of housing, we must admit it has not obtained the success it had hoped for. And after all the cutbacks that this government has been trying to make lately in all sectors, more specifically in the social affairs sector, now on the fever of an election the government in a supreme effort tries to make Canadians believe that it has finally found the answer. This bill is a lot a fuss for nothing. Indeed, what does the government risk with this bill? What does it risk through this proposal as a whole?
I read the first part of the bill. I was not here when the minister delivered the first part of his speech. But I put it aside
Housing
at once because the minister was not dealing with the subject at all; obviously he was upset. He was upset by the vote that has been held and he lost his cool and used some pretty strong words. I shall not repeat them. Recently he wanted me to withdraw my words but I will not ask him to withdraw his. Next time, I suggest he behave in a more dignified manner even if he does not like the result of some votes. Indeed, I do not like to hear these kinds of remarks in the House.
But I found very interesting the second part of his speech with which I shall now deal. I was indeed saying: what is the government risking with this bill? It is risking backing mortgages and perhaps also having to pay out $5 or $10 a month for some tenants who will have trouble paying their rent with its proposal to grant 25 or 30 per cent to those who will spend more than 25 per cent of their income on rent. The real problem is that the federal government is operating in an area outside its jurisdiction, an area coming under provincial jurisdiction. 1 am still wondering why it is so stubborn as to remain in those areas when all the provinces are asking it to withdraw, to let them do as they wish and give them at the same time-
To get out!

Yes, it should get out and at the same time give back the taxation right it has taken. At the present time they have no choice but to provide the money because they have the power of taxation which they borrowed and have been keeping for 38 years. There is the difficulty. There is the problem.
I heard the hon. member say a while ago: Well, the federal government should re-establish they had the nerve to create a Department of Urban Affairs, imagine, when it is a well known fact that urban affairs come under provincial jurisdiction! Well, besides the fact that this is outside its jurisdiction, the government does not know anything about that because it is too far removed from it. It does not, like the provinces, live close to the authorities which are responsible for those municipalities.
The government is anxious to be forgiven for its illegal interference with provincial jurisdiction, and then it hands out goodies to prevent the taxpayers from shouting out their contempt. Why is this government refusing to transfer the powers of taxation to the provinces so that they may administer their affairs within their own area of jurisdiction? You have never seen a province interfering with federal affairs. You have never seen that. They respect federal jurisdiction but why do we not do the same at the federal level? Why not uphold the Constitution and the meagre rights the provinces were given? For the past 10 years, there has been a steady and increasing encroachment upon provincial jurisdiction. No wonder war has broken out between the federal government and the provinces. That is no wonder. Every Canadian knows that urban affairs, housing, house rehabilitation, like commu-

March 5, 1979
Housing
nity services, are constitutionally matters of provincial jurisdiction.
After snatching direct taxation rights from the provinces in a hypocritical and fraudulent way, this government is taking the initiative because it has the money; it collects, it has every spending power, to ask the provinces to share equally. Those were the taxation rights of the provinces, but they are told: Participate. We are going to use your money to pay for that but put up half in any case. That is all very nice. But it holds on to their means of collecting the necessary taxes. Mr. Speaker, that is the problem and the major cause of all those family quarrels. Add to that the way of redistributing the revenues of direct taxation, either through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, project managers and all those who are appointed by the government to carry out projects-I was just talking to the minister this afternoon about that. I told him there were pretty bad things. I know the minister cannot control everything going on in those projects, rehabilitation projects, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation projects and others where you have to qualify and where qualifying means being a Liberal. Well, Mr. Speaker, that I will not forgive. I am not accusing the minister here because 1 know he is not aware of that but things are going on that are unforgivable.
I have seen projects granted to people who had no use for them at all and I have seen other people who would have needed them but failed to qualify because they were probably Conservatives or Social Crediters. I call things as I see them. That must be brought in the open. I am here to say what is going wrong-that also helps the minister, I am sure he is going to keep his eyes open. I told him: "When you select a man like that, I understand that he is on your side, but select three of them and form a committee to prevent discrimination like that". I think that this would immediately clear up the situation and provide everyone with a bit of justice.
In his remarks the minister told us that the current housing programs undertaken in co-operation with the provinces are supplying 19,000 housing units a year, which, again according to the minister, is not sufficient and I agree on that. I also agree on the non-profit housing program. The government expects to build 30,000 units, and the minister adds that the program will be the responsibility of the federal government, the provinces, the municipalities and private or public organizations which may be involved in housing. First, I wonder if the government did meet with the provinces, if it did meet with those who are concerned, with those who are really responsible, if it had discussions with them, because once again as ever it seems to have followed the usual rule, that is to set up the whole program and later submit it to the provinces and say: "Take it or don't take it. If you don't take it, you won't have it; if you do take it, you must follow our rules and do what we tell you to do."

Mr. Speaker, they will have to mend their ways if they are to face the electorate in our provinces, and especially in the province of Quebec, because I can tell them people know what the Liberals are all about. They will get a surprise, not us. The government forgets they use three tax collectors for federal taxes, for provincial taxes and for municipal taxes. This makes for three tax collectors preying on the same taxpayer. The same taxpayer that will be taxed three times is the worker. Always the worker.
Programs are put forward, Quebec and other provinces put them forward in their jurisdictions, but in the final analysis, the worker pays-one, two, three, go! Three taxes for one area or one project. We may not be fully aware of this, but the taxpayer knows. He sees that. I would even say that all those parallel bureaucracies, we will have to get rid of. Each level will have to remain in its own area. The federal government in its area, provinces in their areas, and then only can harmony set in.
The bottom line truth is that the government recognizes it has no more money. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has no more money either. So the government calls upon voluntary organizations, the private sector to hide its failure in housing. The minister suggests that low income people, single mothers, senior citizens will benefit from the program. Admittedly those groups will be able to find easy housing for some time just until the bureaucrats, the "taxers", decide otherwise. We know what goes on in low rental housing.
Senior citizens, as the minister suggested, will get 25 or 30 per cent to help pay their rents where they exceed 25 per cent of their monthly incomes. That is all right, Mr. Speaker, 25 per cent of monthly income, that looks like a nice grant. But what does that mean in actual figures? This is what I am interested in. What does that get us to? Let us take the case of two senior citizens, both getting the old age pension. A couple getting $600 per month in pensions and paying $200 in rent. If they pay a $200 rent on $600 per month, this means they will get nothing. No grant. He might as well not expect it, he will never get it! If his rent is $225 per month, he will get the enormous amount of $6.50 a month, as a tax credit to help him survive. That is the mouse brought forth by the elephant scheme of the minister. What about heating? The rent is taken in consideration. We talk about subsidizing the rent, but what about heating and the other maintenance costs? The new housing units accepted by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation all have electrical heating systems. I know people who had to pay over $800 for heating, last year, in houses accepted by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which were not properly insulated. The contractor probably had some friends working for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That happened before. But, there again, the tenant has to pay for all this. When you feel a draught while sitting by a window, you know there was no insulation.
March 5, 1979

And this was accepted by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which, like others lenders still charges 10 per cent, 1OV2 per cent, 11 per cent, 11'A per cent interest. What about tenants' taxes, Mr. Speaker? I think that the best tax credit should be used to reimburse the municipal taxes paid by tenants in order to avoid double taxation.
If the government reimbursed municipal taxes to tenants, and if we consider the situation of the single family dwelling owner, it is even worse, Mr. Speaker. For years now, we have been urging this government to allow the small home owners to deduct their school and municipal taxes from their income tax and to grant a tax credit to welfare recipients because some home owners are on welfare. Someone earlier was blaming the Progressive Conservative party for asking for a reduction of municipal taxes, but we have been blamed for that for the last 17 years. Yes, 17 years! I really wonder why the home owner is denied a tax credit for municipal and school taxes, for the interest paid on his mortgage interest when it is granted to multiple unit dwelling owners.
Let us suppose that 1 decide to built a 40-unit apartment building, I shall be allowed to deduct from my income tax the interest on my loan plus school and municipal taxes. But this tax relief is denied to the family head who builds a house, the rationale being that he builds for himself. But he does not, he builds for his wife and his children. If he were alone, he would not need a house, he could board somewhere. I think that someone should be entitled to deduct municipal and school taxes as do those who build apartment buildings, it should be him. I fail to understand the logic of this government when it says: "You must not go over that level for fear of becoming too strong and a threat to us. Such reasoning has to be prompted by a desire to squash the low income people. But it does not do them any harm to put up the financing for they are the ones who supply the campaign funds. I call this discrimination. Those who do not pay any income tax are to get a tax credit? Those on welfare already get an allowance for their rent. They should build themselves small inexpensive houses and use this allowance to make their payments. But for God's sake, let us give them a tax credit, and also to the tenants. By the way, the tenants get one from the school board now. This should be in the form of a tax credit which could be surrendered to the municipality since the municipality obviously needs adequate revenue.
In behaving the way it does, Mr. Speaker, the government acts as if it is only interested in making money, in having the poor help increase its own wealth and make the poor even poorer.
The minister says that the National Housing Act is amended to increase the construction of public housing by non-profit organizations. Once again, his objective is praiseworthy, I agree, I support his proposal, but how can that objective be
Housing
reached? By paying once again for four houses to acquire one. If we apply to financial institutions, if we use means made available through the government, even the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which is a government organization, will make you pay the price of four houses to get one. The minister would have a fine opportunity to follow the example of the people. Since non-profit corporations are involved, all voluntary workers who will be unpaid, that is the group that will build low-rental accommodations, could take advantage of interest-free funds. No, they will have to apply to the Bank of Canada exactly as if they were needy countries. There are also needy families and areas. We need not go to other countries to see people in need, Mr. Speaker, there are lots of them in Canada. I think that if the Bank of Canada can help others, it can also help the people of this country.
I will not insist on that lest someone starts talking about the floating dollar. Fortunately the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is not here with his floating dollar or rather his sinking dollar. We cannot bring the dollar back to the surface without upsetting the large financial institutions. The minister also extends the invitation to private investors but when I hear that I wonder whether the government is still willing to keep its word. Again, I blame the minister, but I should not blame him. I should blame the developers because I have evidence about people who took a risk in the private industry, who built 40 units because they had been promised benefits of $80 to $85 per unit and who received only $42 per unit once the work had been done.
So I suggest if we continue to invite private enterprise this way, private entrepreneurs will stay home. And I urge them to stay home as long as the government fails to keep its promise. It gave $89 to others and then only $42 to this one, why? Let us find out. But I talked to the minister about this and I hope he will be fair to him and give him the same amount he gave others, since he made the same effort; he even made more because he was forced to build in winter, which cost him around 10 to 15 per cent more. And when he woke up the next morning with only $42 instead of $89 in rebate, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, this does not encourage future owners at all.
Mr. Speaker, the minister also said he will encourage cooperatives. I do not know what he did for co-operatives, but when he said that, I was reading a press report from today, March 5, and I quote:
Mr. Ouellet wants to kill Quebec's housing co-operatives.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: That is not true.

The minister says it is not true, but I am not the one who said so. Frankly I wonder what happened because here is what we can read in that article:
In an interview with the Journal de Montreal, Mr. Jean-Guy Lague, the spokesman for Quebec housing co-operatives, stated "that the CMHCs new

March 5, 1979
Housing
programs go directly against the basic principles of the present movement of housing co-operatives".
"If the minister had wanted to kill Quebec housing co-operatives, he could not have done any better," added Mr. Lague.
That is PQ propaganda.

Mr. Lague is not a PQ partisan. The hon. member is wrong, because whenever anything happens they yell PQ. You have unemployment, they blame the PQ. People are getting sick, they blame the PQ. You have smallpox and they blame the PQ. That is a sickness now. If you need a psychiatrist, you will be sent to Dr. Laurin .. .

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member know Mr. Lague?
He is not a PQ member.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member know him?
He must be a Social Credit supporter.

I will not say anything because you will be influenced again. Nor I will say he is a Progressive Conservative because you will be influenced again. I continue the quotation:
The housing co-ops are not a new issue. Indeed for several months the Quebec housing co-ops representatives have been trying in vain to meet with Mr. Ouellet.
That is strange because we get to see him any time we want. Simply get him upset a little bit and there he is. I continue:
But the minister delays rendezvous for weeks and weeks. According to that spokesman, the autonomy of co-operatives is not respected when it comes to selecting members and criteria used 10 determine an equitable rent structure.
They also have rental problems, Mr. Speaker.
This new program gives a deadly blow to home rehabilitation by co-op members or working parties. The lower rehabilitation costs as a result of the work performed by co-op members do not reduce the rent but rather the CMHC subsidy.
I am getting close to the point, Mr. Speaker. It seems that when the co-op members volunteer to work on the project, the subsidy is reduced, as he explains, and I quote:
The lower rehabilitation costs as a result of the work performed by co-op members...
-voluntary work-
... do not reduce the rent but rather the CMHC subsidy. It is a program which favours new conduction, unsuitable for buyers of older homes in need of rehabilitation and more suitable to the needs of other provinces. Generally speaking, it is a discriminatory program towards Quebec. What Mr. Ouellet proposes to the Quebec co-operatives are actually "subsidies to the banks" . ..
In that respect, I fully agree with him because those who will benefit from that are precisely the banks, because they will make loans and will never lose a cent. It is the government which guarantees every cent of every mortgage dollar. Therefore, it is true that these are actually subsidies paid to banks. I go on with the quotation:

... it is to reinject co-operative housing into the main stream of the inflationary market, it is to base the development of co-operative housing on the incomes of certain groups of people. In view of the minister's contempt for their proposals, Quebec co-operatives are requesting another meeting with him to ascertain once and for all how these new federal programs will be implemented in regard to the specific features of Quebec housing co-operatives.
Another article refers to a major fight, and I will not have time to read it all because my time is almost expired, but I simply want to say to the minister that if there are falsehoods in the release, I hope he will schedule another meeting, because these people are complaining that they cannot meet with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: I have met with them.

In any event, I told them that if they cannot see him, they can come and see me, and that I know how to arrange a meeting.
Mr. Speaker, the minister asked me for suggestions this afternoon; the best thing I could suggest to him would be to reduce interest rates or, particularly for non-profit projects, to recover only administration costs. This we can do, if we only want to.
Should the government take these means to give satisfaction to senior citizens and low income earners once again, should elections be called, it would be presentable in the province. It must act fast however because the election is getting near and we would like it to be somewhat presentable. We are, for our part, doing our best always, and we will again do our best in the next election. Our organization is such that we can make it known under all its aspects, but I hope they will act before the election is called.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. As far as the Chair is concerned there is, in principle, no list; every member has to rise to seek the floor and the Chair has already recognized the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe. I understand the hon. member's preoccupation. This debate may continue for some while-I do not know what may happen in the House. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe may not be long, and there is a possibility that the hon. member will get an opportunity to speak afterwards.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind my colleague opposite that I will only
March 5, 1979

speak fifteen or twenty minutes. I think that he will have enough time to speak following my comments on the bill.
For several reasons, Mr. Speaker, I would like to support the amendments to the National Housing Act proposed in that bill. I heard my colleague opposite, the previous speaker, say that the bill would have bad implications and that it would be misunderstood by the people. This has surely been already pointed out, but I would like to remind him of some statistics recently provided during a Gallup poll which indicated that in 1963, 76 per cent of the people were satisfied and that today 86 per cent of the people are satisfied with the policies of the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation. In the province of Quebec, 95 per cent of the people are satisfied while 5 per cent are not.
I believe that these recently published figures show that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has done a lot for the building industry and the development of Canada. Indeed, I believe that it represents a logical way to deal with the whole area of housing problems. I am especially pleased to see that this bill has retained one of the most important measures ever implemented in Canada in this area, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program better known as the RRAP.
I am also happy, Mr. Speaker, to see that the restrictions imposed upon this program have been abolished and that it will no longer be limited to certain designated areas. If this bill is passed, as I am sure that it will, Mr. Speaker, all Canadians will be able to benefit from the assistance granted under the RRAP. Under the terms of this program, the available funds will no doubt help to meet the most urgent needs of Canadians throughout the country. I am not surprised that the RRAP has been received so enthusiastically and spontaneously by Canadian as a whole.
I was told that since this program was established in 1973, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has helped in the rehabilitation of approximately 20,000 dwellings a year in Canada. I hope that this figure will increase as the program is expanded and municipal authorities become more familiar with it. Since my election on October 16, just four months ago, my constituency office in St. Hyacinthe has been visited by a great many people asking information about these programs. I could also tell the minister and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation authorities that there is perhaps a lack of information in rural municipalities, who are informed either through the county boards or by material and letters sent to the mayors or the secretaries of these municipalities. I believe that it would be a good thing to familiarize people with Bill C-29 now under consideration.
We must not forget however that housing rehabilitation is a long-term project. About 2 million Canadian dwellings were built before the end of the Second World War. Some of these dwellings are still solid enough while others are not worth being repaired. A basic renovation would do for many of them, perhaps half of them, and would extend their life for many
Housing
years. What I mean, Mr. Speaker, is that a task of such a scope cannot be realized overnight, nor even within a year. The number of houses which can be renovated each year depends not only on the funds that the federal government will be able to allocate to these programs but on the attitude of the municipal organizations which will administer them and of course of the qualified and unionized labour which will be available and capable of making the necessary repairs and restoration works. Undoubtedly the number of renovated houses in Canada is rising each year. I am certain that the government of Canada will go on playing a leading role in this growing industry which is so important for our country. One recognizes more and more in Canada and everywhere in the world that the rehabilitation of dwellings is of capital import. If we think of the energy crisis, of oil and gas restrictions, we see that we must take all possible steps to look after those old houses which, when they were built, did not have any of the insulation which is available to us in the 1980s.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, people in increasing numbers consider that it is better to try and maintain their house and prolong its life expectancy than to take it apart and start from scratch. Renovation and preservation are both important factors of the federal government's conservation policy which calls for the proper administration and recycling of our non-renewable resources. To make a house last longer instead of starting from square one will result in major savings in terms of energy, material and money. And that is more and more what people are seeking both in Canada and elsewhere. In other words, Mr. Speaker, people are more concerned with providing adequate lodging than reaching set goals for housing starts every year.
Mr. Speaker, ever since the end of World War II and up to these past few years, we were mostly concerned with the production and construction of new housing. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was created in 1946 to help us catch up with the backlog accumulated during the depression and war years. But times change and so do the housing needs of Canadians. That factor, Mr. Speaker, associated with many others will mean that fewer new housing units will be needed each year. As we all know, we will probably need only about 20,000 housing starts a year around 1985, as compared with 30,000 today. The decrease in the population growth will also mean the population will be made up of a higher percentage of older persons.
At the same time, people are increasingly putting off getting married and having children, and children are leaving home at an earlier age. As a result of those trends, Mr. Speaker, families are growing smaller and couples without children are becoming more numerous. There will be a resulting exodus from the suburbs and big family houses to downtown areas where housing is older and in greater need of renovation. The increasing cost of gas and decreasing energy resources will in addition speed up this movement towards the city by pushing up the cost of daily commuting.

March 5, 1979
Housing
Mr. Speaker, all those demographic trends and economic projections, as well as changing social values, lead one to believe that rehabilitation will become increasingly important, at least until the end of the 20th century. I am very happy indeed that the government, by introducing these changes, recognizes the importance of renovation programs and the conservation of houses, and that it should have reaffirmed its intention of continuing to support those programs in concrete ways as it does through Bill C-29.
A few words now, Mr. Speaker, about non-profit corporations. I feel that through these assistance programs for cooperative housing projects and non-profit corporations, this bill underlines the needs of those for whom buying decent housing is a must. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that once the bill is passed and implemented, those programs will do much in achieving our objective for people of limited means. I am particularly happy with those programs which merge private capital with federal subsidies, and so achieve an efficient association of the resources of both the private and the public sectors. At this juncture, those financial arrangements are particularly important as government expenditures must be severely restricted for all programs it is setting up.
About those non-profit organizations, Mr. Speaker, I must say that in a riding like Saint-Hyacinthe with some 37 municipalities, already several municipal councils, several non-profit corporations have been formed and have come to ask me for information about those projects scheduled for 1979, having heard that under the new Bill C-29 they could have the benefit of a 100 per cent loan guarantee for non-profit corporations and have to pay only 2 per cent interest whatever the current rate of interest at the time the contract is signed. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that in a riding like Saint-Hyacinthe, at least five municipalities are already interested in that proposal, and I believe the publicity about this bill will have to be toned down for a while because we will surely not be able to have them all go ahead during 1979-80. I also say to the minister that projects will be welcome on the south shore of Montreal.
We also have in the town of Saint-Hyacinthe itself, Mr. Speaker, a 137-unit project under completion which should be opened in the month of March. The municipal authorities in Saint-Hyacinthe are asking us to apply for a new project because demand being so strong for retired people, this 137-unit project is already filled to capacity.
Mr. Speaker, 1 must say also that the housing policy set out in this bill is much wiser, fairer and much more efficient than certain irresponsible proposals put forward by members of the official opposition. I am thinking for example, Mr. Speaker, about the idea of making mortgage interest and municipal taxes deductible from taxable income. That proposal is in my opinion irresponsible because it is being introduced at a time when the government with the support and the approval of business is making big efforts to reduce spending and deficit. And members opposite chose precisely that time to put for-

ward a measure that would cost hundreds of millions of dollars and would actually benefit only a very limited group of people who are far from being those most in need of help.
Out of the seven and a half million families in Canada, about three million rent either out of necessity or by choice. The tax deduction being proposed by certain members of the opposition will be of no use to that group in which you find most needy families. Approximately 2.5 million Canadians are home owners paying off mortgages. Among them are not only low income Canadians who were assisted in purchasing their homes but also the richest people in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I think the bill before us provides assistance to all Canadians, because it gives them the opportunity to buy good homes at a price they can afford. Given the present economic situation in the country, this legislation is socially equitable and financially sound. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is highly preferable to the inequitable, irresponsible, discredited yet revived proposal put forth by members of the opposition.
Mr. Speaker, there is a saying to the effect that activity in the building trade is a sign of prosperity, yet when we look at the latest figures for housing starts, we see that there were only 227,667 housing starts in 1978 as compared to 254,725 in 1977. The number of completed homes in 1978 came down to 246,653 units compared with 251,789 in 1977. So there has been a decrease in construction in 1978, and we must do everything possible, Mr. Speaker, to boost the construction industry in the province of Quebec as well as in the whole country.

Mr. Speaker, I have enjoyed listening to this debate, particularly the remarks of the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) who, in true Liberal fashion, came down four square solidly on all sides. On the one hand he is in against the bill, and on the other hand he is in favour of it. He did not like the fact that his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), issued a fiat to the effect that this department will be abolished, but he is going to vote for the bill anyway. The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) was right when he said the government had no business in this business in the first place. Over the past ten or twelve years, experience has shown that it should never have gone into it. There are a lot of sorry home owners in Canada who have had the disagreeable experience of buying homes under some of the more unfortunate schemes this department put together.
The intent of Bill C-29 was well capsulized by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) who has a talent for compressing a comprehensive subject into a very few sentences. On March 1, as reported at page 3742 of Hansard, he said:
Essentially, the bill does three things. First, it disentangles the mess which the government has created in housing at both provincial and municipal levels over the last seven years; second, it cuts out the government's Financial commitment
March 5, 1979

to housing and urban affairs and, third, it winds down the Ministry of Urban Affairs after its death was announced in 1978. That is really what the bill does on behalf of the government. It disentangles, it cuts losses, and it winds down the ministry.
In a nutshell, that is what the bill is all about, but that really does not tell the history of some of the experiences people have had with this department.
I remember, when I came to this House almost five years ago, listening to the former minister of housing and urban affairs who is now the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson). Every year he would give statistics for the new housing starts-20,000, 30,000-they all looked good and it sounded as if the needs of the Canadian people were being met. It was evident that he was very statistics conscious, as I am sure the present minister is. It took two or three years for the reactions to those statistics on AHOP to come in. The big problem with AHOP is that it is not a "people" program. It was just another public relations gimmick, made to sound great, fun to end load the thing, to make sure that people could afford the downpayment. All the new housing starts to meet the needs of the people would make the government look good, and actually its purpose was to meet the public relations needs of the government. It took three or four years for us to find out what was going on. While this bill gets rid of the original department, it does not get rid of the problem, Mr. Speaker.
Some of my constituents who talked to me about the AHOP program showed me a brochure from CMHC which said that the government inspection would look after things. I notice that the bill does not change that. Clause 1(a) reads as follows:
(a) in accordance with this Act make approved loans on such security in favour of the lender as is provided for by this Act;
Mark those words, Mr. Speaker, "in favour of the lender." That is why I say it is not a people program.
It is called free enterprise.

The hon. member from Saskatchewan, who has never had a housing problem in his province because nobody ever moves there, wants to educate everybody else on what should be done about housing. I understand there is zero population growth in Saskatchewan. I would say that the lenders, the trust companies, mortgage companies and the banks, are big enough to look after themselves. Surely the Royal Bank, the Bank of Montreal or the Bank of Nova Scotia and all the trust companies have enough resources to supply their own inspectors.
The first-time home buyer who reads that brochure is starry eyed at the prospect of moving into a new home and thinks he is going to be protected. It is not the home buyer who is protected by that inspection, Mr. Speaker, it is the lender, and those lenders are big enough to look after themselves. The bill does nothing to correct that and I think the minister ought to change it so that it does. If inspections are necessary, and they are, why should they not be done on behalf of the buyer rather than on behalf of the money lender?
Housing
The second area in which this is not a "people" policy is that a ceiling is put on the price of the homes, especially in AHOP projects. At first blush that looks good. A buyer does not have to pay more than $47,000 for a home and that seems to be an advantage to the first-time home buyer. While it imposes a ceiling on the price of the home, however, it in no way imposes a ceiling on the cost to the contractor. It costs him just as much to buy the lumber, provide the services and pay the subtrades. The bill does not impose a ceiling on the cost of production, but only on the cost to the purchaser.
If the contractor is to meet that cost price squeeze he must look for ways of doing it, and it is likely that he will try to get money above the ceiling. Of course this is not legitimate.
On Saturday morning when I was in my riding I received a call from a constituent who claimed that he had not slept all night. The evening before he had signed an agreement to purchase an AHOP home. After he signed, the realtor slipped another piece of paper to him on which was written "lot differential fee". It turned out that in this project the original plans had not been good enough to suit the municipality and the developer was asked to upgrade them, which of course cost more. In an effort to recoup he put this piece of paper before the buyer and told him not to show it to his banker, otherwise he might not approve the mortgage.
I asked for a copy of the documents which I said I would take to the minister, as I did. To the credit of the former minister he said this was not right, and got in touch with his officials in Vancouver regarding the matter. Before the day was out, that project was frozen and about 35 home buyers had their money refunded.
When a ceiling is put on the price of the home, with no way of controlling the cost to the contractor, he is going to try to make it make it up in some other way. He can make it up by cutting corners. That is fine, as long as they are not cut so much as to produce a shoddy piece of merchandise.
The former minister was so interested in statistics that he put pressure on CMHC officials to get the contractors involved in this program. They were supposed to get out and build the homes. The result was that the good reputable contractors who had been in business for a long time and were concerned about their reputation and about ethics, stayed away from the program for the first two or three years. Meanwhile the quick operators moved in, put together a land assembly and, because there was no proper surveillance, they cut costs.
In a project in my constituency there were about 35 homes. I have shown the minister a video tape of some of the things that are wrong with it. He says it is too bad, that it should not be that way, and indicated that his officials in Vancouver say it is not right. It does not look as though the people concerned are going to get anything out of it, however. They have lost thousands of dollars in these homes but are not going to get anything from the government. I visited those people who bought some of those AHOP homes, Mr. Speaker.

March 5, 1979
Housing
In one case I know I hit my head on the dining room chandelier near the fridge. Would you believe that in a number of cases there was an electric splice box with bare wires? These were located behind medicine cabinets directly above the sinks. Just for kicks someone said, "I bet I can short that out." The man took a screwdriver to one of the boxes and blew out the fuse. This was a CMHC inspected home. Then there were water problems to contend with. These included seepage of water into the basement and water running into the basement instead of away from the house. The design did not call for closet doors, and there were none. Every closet door was a different size. Now it costs the home buyer twice as much, perhaps even three times as much to buy closet doors. In another home one had to open the oven door in order to get the cutlery drawer open. The list goes on and on.
The government inspectors were not doing their job. The former minister was so anxious to get statistics in order that he could have his 20,000, 25,000 and 30,000 new homes each year that he sacrificed the home buyer in the process. What we had was a series of companies throughout the country which were forming new companies to develop one project. They would then build all the homes and move out, taking the assets from the company and finally dissolving it, so that there was no way the homeowners could ever touch that company again. This happened because the minister was in a hurry. We have CMHC saying that they will secure the mortgage. But they made sure those homes were just good enough so they would last the life of the 25-year mortgage. Who knows what will happen after that?
Instant slums.

Instant slums, right. Why were there not more inspectors? I understand from officials that they could not hire enough of them, first, because the growth factor was so large and, second, because the turnover rate in the inspection department was so great they could not train people fast enough to take care of the inspections. But, the minister got his statistics. Is it any wonder that as a result of AHOP now, after five years of production, out of 130,000 AHOP units built between 1973 and 1978 we have 53,000 units unsold? This amounts to roughly 35 per cent to 40 per cent unsold. Who knows how many of them are now vacant because of midnight movers? People said that the payments for the first five years were going to be subsidized, and in the next five years they would have to make that up. But in the next five years the house has already depreciated, so why pay higher payments for a depreciated house? And the midnight movers move in, and the 'for sale' signs go up.
In 1978, 10 per cent of the owners of AHOP homes defaulted on their payments. This compares with one half of 1 per cent of conventional mortgage home owners. That is the human problem. The minister can look at the statistics, and the House can study the statistics. That is one thing, but what about the pain and the anguish of those people who, for the first time, said, "I am going to have my own home."? They

move into their dream home and those dreams are shattered within two years. For about three years there is one project on which I have worked with these people and with the minister and got zilch satisfaction out of it. The latest thing which the minister introduced is a kind of insurance program for new home buyers. That insurance program is about five years late. Incidentally, that insurance program is a confession of failures in other programs.
The other indefinable, intangible problem that this massive failure has created is the problem of reputation. What must it be like for someone who lives in an AHOP home in what has already been described as an AHOP district when he has to try to hide from other people that he lives in an AHOP project?
Reputable contractors have been coming on stream and they have been sharpening their pencils. They have said, "Look, if I do this and this, I think I can put out a new product within the price the ceiling establishes." So there are a lot of good AHOP projects around. The people who have bought in these projects are satisfied. They have a good reputation, except blurred across that good reputation are the other AHOP projects that people want nothing to do with. These include homes that were bought for $47,000 and are now worth perhaps $45,000, $44,000 or even $43,000. These homes were for first time home buyers. People not only had to come up with the down payment, which was hard to come by because obviously this program was designed for low income home owners, but frequently they had to borrow that down payment either from the bank, relatives or friends. Once they are in these homes they have to borrow more money for upgrading purposes so the houses will look the way they were supposed to look in the first place.
There is this mixed picture of good AHOP projects, mediocre AHOP projects, and poor AHOP projects. There is blurring in the public's mind. Where is the home buyer at in a situation like this? What do we do?
Now that the program seems to be working, as this government so often does, it has cancelled the program. That is it. It did this with the assisted rental program. Then it moves into another new area. The government's new alternative to AHOP is a graduated mortgage payment. It simply says that if one cannot afford a steep down payment, "We want to help you with that and temporarily ease the burden." In other words, in the first five years the burden will not seem quite so bad, but in the second five years it will get worse.
The government has ensured that inflationary pressures will continue. It is building on inflation on the one hand. In all the other programs it is saying, "We are trying to fight inflation, we are going to reduce inflation from 9 per cent to 7 per cent to 6.5 per cent." The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is continually saying, "We are going to cut it down." But in a program like the graduated mortgage payment program it is saying, "Inflation is going to be here a long time. We are going to help you fight inflation by helping you with this graduated mortgage payment." By so-called levelling out these payments it is increasing the inflationary pressures for these people who are buying these homes.
March 5, 1979

I note with interest comments of an earlier speech in this debate where the speaker quoted one of the economists in this country. At page 3746 of Hansard for March 1, 1979, it reads:
Administered by the CMHC, GMP's are designed to give a house buyer one of the major advantages already provided by AHOP during the first five years of a graduated payment mortgage, monthly payments are much lower than a conventional mortgage would allow. From then on, payments are stepped up gradually until after the tenth year, when they reach a plateau.
The economist was a good man with figures, and he whipped out his pocket calculator. He found out that this was not such a great deal for the home buyer. As he said, the unpleasant, less obvious fact is that over the life of the debt the graduated mortgage payment will cost the borrower $9,324 more than the standard mortgage would, $105,024 compared to $95,700. As the speaker said at that time, the man who buys this mortgage borrows $35,000 and he pays back $105,024. Who needs that kind of help? Not the first time home buyer.
The economist goes on to call this permadebt. He will never get out of debt. It used to be that a man's home was his castle. It is now the case that the government is going to make sure that a man's home is somebody else's castle. The home buyer will never look forward to the day when he can own his own home.
I do not know that we can afford in this country to encourage a policy of debtorship. I thought in this country we were proposing policies of ownership, not debtorship, but the government seems to insist on wanting to lay the burden on those who cannot afford it so that they will be perpetually in debt, never seeing daylight. It believes in debtorship, not ownership.
A number of government members have criticized the Conservative plan to introduce deductibility of mortgage payments and home owner taxes from income tax.
They just wish they had thought of it first.

That's right, they wish they had. Now they are fighting a rear guard action and spending all their time trying to find fault with something they wanted to promote previously. That is not easy.
The latest gimmick is to say that members from both sides of the House visited Washington where everyone was against the program. I lived in the United States for about seven years and I remember the home owners talking about that. There was not one who was not claiming it on their income tax. They thought it was the greatest thing to happen since sliced bread. At least it led to home ownership.
And early.

As the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Hare) says, it leads to home ownership early. There were people in Washington who were against it, the same type of people as those in Ottawa who are against it, those in the department of HEW, the housing department. The bureaucrats think it is their God-given right to collect all the taxes in the country and to be the omniscient dispensers of tax money
Housing
in programs which they design, programs which they believe are infallible. In Washington, as in Ottawa, they believe they know best how to spend the tax dollars.
They get advice from tax lawyers.
That is right, those who specialize in that kind of mentality.
They make a lot of money.
That's right.
How much help do you need?

I will take all the help I can get from the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) because it is good. I don't mind. The Liberals are saying this does not work well. When something has worked for 30 or 40 years in the United States and they say it does not work, I wonder about their rationale. We are making a proposal to the people of Canada. So that those who need it most will benefit the most, all those up to a level of $50,000 will be able to deduct their mortgage interest rate from their income tax.
I just finished a survey in my constituency. One of the questions I asked was. are you in favour of being able to deduct housing interest payments and property taxes from your income tax? Surprise, surprise, 81 per cent of those who responded were in favour.
I love it.

There is one of those rich Liberals who will make use of this. 1 do not think the minister of amateur sport should get involved in this. She has not yet solved the coastal transportation problems. Therefore, she should not get into the housing debate.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext: You had better stick to AHOP.
I am sorry AHOP ever came into Surrey.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext: Ask your mayor.

I have, and don't think we haven't been talking about it. As a matter of fact, the whole GVRD looked at the AHOP program and you know what they thought about it. This is the minister who said she was going to resign if in 90 days the transportation problems along the northern coast was not solved. She must have invented the metric calendar because that 90 days was up three years ago and she is still hanging around.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext: Go back to Surrey. They don't want AHOP in their boundaries.

She is now taking the expertise she gained solving all the northern transportation problems and is investing her expertise in Loto Canada where she has managed to lose $13 million. Now she wants to help in housing problems.

March 5, 1979
Adjournment Debate
Members of this House, I do not think we need that kind of help from the minister of amateur fitness.
The Liberal members want to draw up a list as long as your arm listing all the reasons the program we have devised will not work. Although they are against it, millions of home owners across Canada are in favour of it, and they are going to see that we have a chance to bring about that policy and provide them with the kind of help for which they are looking.
If there is ever an election.
That's right. There is another suggestion that I think is interesting. Something like 400,000 home owners in this country spend over 30 per cent of their income on housing.
They own homes though.

Can they afford them? The CMHC guideline states that you should never spend more than 25 per cent. The government is breaking its own guideline and allowing CMHC mortgages to people paying more than 30 per cent of their income. There are something like 800,000 home owners who spend over 25 per cent of their income on housing.
We have a situation where 1,200,000 home owners in this country spend more than 25 per cent of their income on housing. We in the Conservative party have a solution to that problem. If the Prime Minister gets the nerve to call an election we will be able to present that solution. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, so that I can finish tomorrow?
