subtopic: LABOUR DISPUTES-ACTION TAKEN TO AVERT POSSIBLE STRIKE OF VANCOUVER DOCK WORKERS

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: LABOUR DISPUTES-ACTION TAKEN TO AVERT POSSIBLE STRIKE OF VANCOUVER DOCK WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in connection with questions I raised last Friday in the House during the question period with respect to some of the difficulties being experienced by our grain transportation system. I know that we often rise in this House for the purpose of trying to get better answers to some of the questions we put in question period, but I am in the awkward position of having taken the exceptional step of giving notice of my intention to ask a question, explaining to the minister precisely what I was going to ask, and having the parliamentary secretary get up and tell me that he would take notice of my question. That is what I would term the ultimate in unsatisfactory answers as far as a question very important to western Canada is concerned.
Quite apart from the fact that grain transportation is vital to the farmer and an efficient grain delivery system is vital to people in western Canada, I should point out these are also vital to the total economy in Canada. I think the government should pay attention to that fact, and when people from western Canada ask questions about such very important topics, the government should understand how important they are to all of Canada. They are not local, parochial, or regional questions at all.
I want to deal this evening with that aspect of my question which related to hours of work regulations under the Canada Labour Code. You will know, Mr. Speaker, that under the amendments to that legislation which were passed in 1977, there has been ongoing consultation between the Department of Labour and western grain elevator operators with respect to whether elevator managers in western Canada are going to be exempted from the hours of work provisions in that legislation, or whether there is going to be some special arrangement for elevator managers, having regard to the unique and seasonal nature of their business in terms of the grain trade. I am sorry to report that there has been no resolution of that very serious matter.
The minister has been out in Western Canada meeting with representatives of elevator companies, pools and others. They have been very dissatisfied with the way in which this matter has been handled as far as the Department of Labour is concerned. In fact the secretary-manager of the Western Grain Elevator Association, Mr. Keith Grey, is quoted as saying that the Western Grain Elevator Association is totally dissatisfied with the proposed hours of work regulations for grain elevator workers. He said:
We are not happy with anything because we feel the managers are exempt and Labour Canada is taking a firm position in opposition of that representation, which we feel is not on sound ground.
The article in which that quotation is printed goes on to say:
He said the minister has met with the association on two separate occasions to explain why country elevator managers "cannot be totally exempt from the hours-of-work provisions of the Canada Labour Code."
"The bureaucrats are not concerned with political ramifications. If we cannot obtain an understanding with the minister through discussion, then we will have to go another route," Grey said.
In another interview Mr. Grey put his finger on the way this problem might be solved. He is quoted in the Western Producer of Thursday, March 1, 1979. The article in which he is quoted reads in part as follows:
A change of government in the next federal election would probably help the grain elevator industry receive a permanent exemption from federal hours of work rules for employees-
If the Progressive Conservatives win, "I think they are in tune with the concerns of western Canada," he said. "It could well mean a total exemption."
Mr. Grey went on to reiterate that the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) understands and is sympathetic to elevator company concerns about hours of work, "but he is getting bad advice from his bureaucrats". The situation is simply that federal proposals to end the exemption have been postponed several times, and the latest postponement came last February

March 5, 1979

15 when implementation was put off from April 15, 1979, to April 15, 1980. The article goes on:
Industry officials have argued that because elevator managers are paid both a base salary and some "incentive bonuses," hours restrictions and overtime would require a major revision of pay structures. It would also require an extensive monitoring and policing system.
I think the worst complaint of the people in the industry and of the people in western Canada is the indecision and lack of sensitivity of the government to the practical circumstances of the western farmer in terms of his relationship with the western grain elevator managers. These people, by and large, are highly industrious, highly efficient managers of western grain elevators, and they perform a very important and useful function within the community. They are available to farmers at a time of their greatest need. They are compensated in terms of incentive bonuses and are given time off to make up for the overtime they put in during the course of a busy season. Probably this is hanging over them as another obstacle to the efficient grain delivery system, so I ask the parliamentary secretary to give us some assurance, and to give some assurance to western Canadians and to the grain elevator managers with regard to the government's intentions, whether or not it is going to play around with the matter indefinitely, causing the kind of inconveniences which have been caused up to this point.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Dennis Dawson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: LABOUR DISPUTES-ACTION TAKEN TO AVERT POSSIBLE STRIKE OF VANCOUVER DOCK WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to extend my apologies to the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) for not answering his second question last Friday, but unfortunately, despite the generous 15 minutes' advice he gave to the minister's office, it had been impossible for me to grasp all the aspects in his question in order to give him a reliable and complete answer. I hope I will be able tonight to give him some elements of answer which will prove to his satisfaction. [English]
Since his appointment last year, the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) has had numerous discussions with representatives of the Western Grain Elevator Association on the hours of work question. The association is fully aware of his position regarding the need to ensure fair treatment of employees. He is also aware of the needs of farmers for extended grain elevator services during the planting and harvest seasons.
Consequently, the Western Grain Elevator Association and the grain services union have now been informed that the current exemption from the hours of work provisions of the Canada Labour Code for country elevator agents, managers and their assistants, due to expire on April 14, 1979, will be extended to April 14, 1980, at which time a modified hours of work regime will come into effect.
The new hours of work regime will take into account the interests of the employees concerned, the interests of farmers and the interests of the grain elevator companies, by providing
Adjournment Debate
for standard hours of work of 48 in a week and a maximum of 60 hours a week during the planting and harvest season, instead of the 40 and 48 hours respectively provided by division I of Part III of the Canada Labour Code.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INQUIRY WHETHER AGREEMENT REACHED WITH NEW BRUNSWICK ON ADDITIONAL DEVELOPMENT
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INQUIRY WHETHER AGREEMENT REACHED WITH NEW BRUNSWICK ON ADDITIONAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday, I asked the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion about the progress made in the negotiations with New Brunswick concerning a subsidiary agreement on so-called developing regions.
These regions include not only my riding of Madawaska-Victoria but also that of Northumberland-Miramichi and the regions of Grand Lake and Charlotte in southern New Brunswick which, as a whole, have not yet been covered by a special agreement as was the case in almost all other regions of the province.
The northeast agreement has been known for years and includes the counties of Restigouche and Gloucester. There was an agreement on the Mactaquac region, the agreement concerning the special zones of St. John and Moncton, the agreement on Kent county, and let us not forget the sectorial agreements on agriculture, forestry, highways and others which of course concern the whole province.
In the circumstances, it was perfectly normal that northwest New Brunswick should claim its fair share. However, I emphasize that my region benefited from the programs offered by the federal government through DREE, the Department of Transport, the Department of Urban Affairs and others. The regional airport, Assomption Crossing in Edmundston, the regional museum, McCain Foods, Nadeau & Nadeau furniture, Fraser plants and dozens of small businesses are just a few examples of a long list of achievements in which the federal government has been involved. However, there is still some basic work to be done and I shall deal with this tonight. There are the municipal infrastructures that are essential to a certain quality of life and conditional to our economic development.
The small municipalities which do not have a large enough tax base to provide a minimum of services are particularly deserving in this regard.
While the northeastern part of the province and urban areas in the south could benefit from generous federal-provincial development agreements, many northwestern municipalities either had to freeze their water and sewer system projects, for instance, or pay through the nose. The provincial government told them: You are wealthy enough, you are well off in the northwest.
3842

March 5, 1979
Adjournment Debate
My colleague from Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) and myself were opposed to these disparities being perpetuated in a province which was already underprivileged compared with the others. We urged the present minister to correct these aberrations and I believe that we have won the first 14 rounds of the match, thanks, I am glad to note, to the understanding and the generosity of the minister, and in spite of the stubborn resistance first shown by the province of New Brunswick which opposed the negotiation of this agreement.
We therefore developed, with the industrial boards of our areas and in close consultation with the municipalities involved, a series of projects and proposals which, if all were accepted, would greatly assist in our industrialization and job creation efforts, without however being a solution to all the problems. This does not mean that all the proposals contained in the draft agreement are equally good or urgent or that the federal and provincial governments have enough money to finance all of them. As usual, the federal government will pay the bigger share, from 75 to 80 per cent, and the province and the municipalities, the taxpayers in other words, will pay the rest.
Unlike certain provincial ministers who represent my area, I do not consider the federal government as an inexhaustible source of funds. I feel particularly distrustful of electoral promises made by provincial politicians who will deliver just about anything and unknowingly feed great expectations into the minds of local governments and communities. The very meaning of the words consultation and negotiation should be explained to these people. Furthermore, it is the provincial government which itself put a ceiling of $25 million on the contribution of the two superior levels of governments in the agreement which we are now negotiating. It is a lot or it is too little. It all depends on which side you are. As for me, Mr. Speaker, what is important is to get started and to reach an agreement as soon as reasonably possible. 1 understand that the federal and provincial governments agree over most of the proposals contained in the draft agreement and that the views vary on one or two projects only.
Orally and in writing I have asked the minister to sign the agreement for the projects on which there is a consensus even if it becomes necessary to add or modify certain aspects later on. The municipalities would like to know the intentions of the two levels of government so as to be able to take advantage of the pleasant season ahead. The minister knows fully well that it takes some time to call the tenders, to study them, to award the contracts, to purchase the materials, to hire the manpower and to get the projects under way.
In answer to my question, last Friday the minister said he hoped that the agreement could be effective as of the next fiscal year. It is also my hope and the Parliamentary Secretary, the honourable member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood), who is going to speak tonight on his behalf and who has been a member of the Atlantic Development Commission, is aware of

the problems of my riding and of the maritimes. I am quite confident that he will be able to provide my constituents and myself with an encouraging answer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Donald Wood (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-INQUIRY WHETHER AGREEMENT REACHED WITH NEW BRUNSWICK ON ADDITIONAL DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have this opportunity to respond to the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin).
In order to provide for special development measures in four New Brunswick regions which are lagging behind the rest of the province, negotiations are nearing completion with the province for the signing of a subsidiary agreement to provide assistance in overcoming intraprovincial disparities. I am aware, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member has discussed this important subject as recently as this afternoon with the minister.
An examination of the distribution of economic activity reveals that each of the regions has a significant reliance on the primary sectors. Growth in the manufacturing sector has not been sufficient to absorb increases in the labour force. The four regions are the following: Northwest-the counties of Madawaska and Victoria; Miramichi-the county of Northumberland; Grand Lake-the counties of Sunbury and Queens; Charlotte-the county of Charlotte.
Rates of population growth in these regions have been typically lower than the provincial average. A contributing factor to the relatively poor population growth is the lack of employment opportunities in these regions. Both average income, and average earned income remain below the respective provincial averages. For the majority of the six counties, the gap is most pronounced for average earned income.
There is little to suggest that these regions, left to their own devices, will significantly alter their relative position vis-a-vis their provincial average. There exists a requirement to revitalize the various regional economies, and to encourage local growth and development. The proposed agreement will attempt to encourage such development by providing funds for specific projects which may have a particularly significant effect on the regional economies.
The agreement proposal has been formulated following a planning and public consultation exercise which has attempted to ensure that initiatives respond to public priorities. Special emphasis has been given to the views of local community business leaders. A series of meetings was held in June and July 1978 in order that development needs and potential could be discussed by representatives of government and those of the designated regions.
A major objective of the agreement will be to halt, and possibly reverse the long-term declining trend in employment and income levels. The proposed programs are intended to take advantage of resource and industrial development opportunities, and reinforce the growth potential of a number of selected centres by the provision of infrastructure assistance.
March 5, 1979

subtopic: TRADE-GATT NEGOTIATIONS ON NON-TARIFF TRADE BARRIERS
TRADE-GATT NEGOTIATIONS ON NON-TARIFF TRADE BARRIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate to follow up a question I put to the minister responsible for DREE, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), on February 28, dealing with his knowledge of the current GATT negotiations. In his response the minister said he was not in a position at that time to report on the progress which had been made with the United States in relation to non-tariff trade barriers.
Unfortunately, time did not permit me to pose my supplementary question. It would have been in line with my proposed motion under the terms of Standing Order 43 for which I had earlier sought unanimous consent. It would have been: "Would the minister consider proposing regionalization schemes and negotiating subsidized exports so that provinces such as New Brunswick could benefit from the lowering of trade barriers with New England and become an attractive location for branch plants?"
I should like to reiterate, for the benefit of the House, that the maritimes and New Brunswick were at one time the hub of economic activity in Canada. It was only after the opening of large markets in central and western Canada that our economy began to decline. It is not the way of maritimers or of Atlantic Canadians to expect others to bear the burden of the social and economic stagnation we have experienced over the past number of years. We possess a good many resources, including people, to deal with our problems.
What has happened is that the Atlantic region and the maritime region have become a bit like a boat, adrift in the sea of economic stagnation, with a broken oar. There are all kinds of statistics to point out the fact that the maritime region and the Atlantic region are indeed a depressed area and, therefore, an area at which this government should take a strong look.
The government's approach has been through DREE and in that respect I give it full credit, although DREE has not solved the problem. It has been in existence for approximately ten years and, indeed, it has allayed our difficulties to some degree. I applaud the government's efforts from the standpoint of realizing that the maritime region does have a particular problem. I want the government to know that, as maritimers, we appreciate the feeling that the government has taken in its approach through DREE.
Unfortunately what has developed since the decentralization of DREE is that there has been no change in its attitudes, no gut changes in its approach. This has contributed to the continuing attitude of the Bay Street mandarins toward the Atlantic region, an attitude which I refer to as a "piggy bank" attitude. I feel that there should be a definite plank for development. I believe that DREE should take upon itself a program to establish definite goals that would illustrate the direction in which it would like to see the Atlantic region go. I believe that a fresher approach is necessary, and I would like
Adjournment Debate
to see new life injected into the old program and hierarchy of DREE.
Let me now refer to the present GATT negotiations. I am not privy to any inside information, but I believe that one approach which could be taken to help develop the Atlantic region would be to negotiate with the United States with regard to the maritime and Atlantic regions specifically. The Atlantic region is hindered in taking advantage of the great New England market, which is comprised of millions of people, by the economic countervailing duties, trade barriers, and so on.
I would like to see the day when DREE could be disbanded altogether. I suggest that one approach would be to set up a special program whereby products which are manufactured and exported from the maritime region to the New England market are given special consideration. This would have the benefit of attracting new industry to the maritimes and of inspiring manufacturers to expand existing industry. It would also pave the way for that well known approach which has been talked about for some time, the branch plant approach, whereby major manufacturers in other areas of Canada locate and establish branch plants in an area which has access to particular markets. We offer in this case a well positioned geographic location plus a solid, substantial labour market, so that the products of an industry could be very attractive to that very lucrative New England market.
It was in this context that I posed my question the other day during question period. I appreciate the opportunity of having this allotted time to bring my concerns to the attention of the government, because I am not hindered by the question period in so far as supplementary questions are concerned.
I think that the attitude of the government, although it is channelled in the proper direction, has become stagnated. I would like to see a face lift for DREE, with the ultimate goal of phasing out the operation totally because we, as Atlantic Canadians and maritimers, have the expertise, labour, and certainly the willingness.

speakeroldname: Mr. Donald Wood (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: TRADE-GATT NEGOTIATIONS ON NON-TARIFF TRADE BARRIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to respond to the hon. member on the question of our progress with the United States in the GATT negotiations in Geneva in the area of non-tariff barriers.
The draft agreements that we have been discussing with our trading partners cover a very wide range of subjects-subsidies and countervailing duties, government procurement practices, customs valuation, safeguards against disruptive imports, technical barriers to trade, import licensing procedures, the counterfeiting of commercial trade marks, and trade in civil aircraft and parts. All of these, of course, have been the subject of multilateral discussion rather than direct negotiation with the United States. Given the extent of our trade with that country, however, their impact on the flow of goods between us is clearly of major significance. An obvious example is the code on subsidies and countervailing duties.

March 5, 1979
Adjournment Debate
As a result of these negotiations, the U.S. Congress will be asked to amend its legislation to require a determination of material injury to domestic industry as a precondition to the imposition of countervailing duties. Such a change will substantially diminish the threat of such duties being levied against Canadian exports which have benefited from Canadian assistance programs. This has obvious relevance to the sorts of cases we have encountered in recent months.
In the area of government procurement, what is being discussed is a code which will provide a start in bringing government purchases under international trade discipline. The question of coverage is still under negotiation. With regard to customs valuation, an international code has also been under discussion. As drafted, there remained a number of difficulties from the Canadian point of view. No government decision has yet been taken as to whether or not Canada will adhere to this code and, if so, under what conditions.
Another important area in the negotiations has to do with safeguards, that is to say, the action which a country is permitted to take to protect its domestic producers from serious injury arising from a sudden and significant increase in
imports. One of the special questions under discussion is a provision which would allow such action to be taken on a selective basis against imports from those countries primarily responsible for the injury, rather than against imports from all suppliers of the product in question.
The proposed agreement of technical barriers is designed to prevent the use of standards or technical regulations in such a way as to create unnecessary obstacles to the flow of international trade. Canada and the United States have common interests in this area.
In general, Canada and the United States are in reasonable agreement on these various codes and other arrangements. For the most part they are at a relatively advanced stage and negotiations are continuing. Even after the negotiations are over, of course, there will undoubtedly remain a number of non-tariff problems to be resolved. These will be taken up as necessary with the United States and our other trading partners.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
